nuance.analogy: Explicitness is like a road sign that says EXIT 12 in large letters, rather than a faint hint that you might find an exit somewhere ahead.
nuance.etymology: From explicit, from Latin explicitus, unfolded or made plain, plus the English suffix -ness.
common_mistakes: Stressing the first syllable, as in EK-splis-it-ness.
Using explicitness only for sexual content, when the word simply means clarity of statement.

senses.definition: Of or relating to exportation or exports.
senses.example: The export manager spent all morning on the new shipping paperwork.

senses.definition: Something that is exported.
senses.example: Oil is the main export of Saudi Arabia.

senses.definition: The act of exporting.
senses.example: The export of fish is forbidden in this country.

senses.definition: To carry away.
senses.example: The river slowly exported tons of silt from the hillside into the bay.

senses.definition: To sell (goods) to a foreign country.
senses.example: Japan exports electronic goods throughout the world.

senses.definition: To cause to spread in another part of the world.
senses.example: Some scholars argue that colonial rule exported bureaucratic habits to distant territories.

senses.definition: To send (data) from one program to another.
senses.example: I'll export the survey results to a CSV file so I can open them in R.

senses.definition: To put up (a child) for international adoption.
senses.example: The agency tried to export more children abroad before the new adoption law took effect.

core.definition: A product or service that is sent to another country to be sold there.

pronunciation.tip: As a noun, the stress falls on the first syllable, EK. As a verb the stress moves to the second syllable, ex-PORT, so 'an EXport' and 'to exPORT' differ in stress. The r in port is pronounced in American English.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. In economic discussions it is often positive when it means growth or jobs, and negative when it means losing domestic supply.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use export as a noun in news, business, and economics, as in 'agricultural exports.' Everyday speakers use it when talking about trade or where products come from. The verb is ex-PORT, and it commonly appears in phrases like 'export to Canada.' Note that the noun and verb stress different syllables.

distinctions.note: An import is a product brought into a country from abroad. An export is a product sent out to another country.
A product is any item made or sold. An export is a product defined by being sent to another country.

examples.everyday: Soybeans are one of the biggest American exports, so you see them shipped all over the world.
examples.professional: Our export revenue rose twelve percent after the new distributor signed on in Germany.
examples.analytical: Trade theorists often ask whether an export boom produces economic growth or merely reflects growth that was already underway.

nuance.analogy: An export is like a letter sent overseas: the goods leave home, cross a border, and arrive where someone else will use them.
nuance.etymology: From Latin exportare 'carry out,' from ex- 'out' and portare 'to carry.'
common_mistakes: Using the verb stress on the first syllable, 'EX-port,' when the verb is ex-PORT.
Confusing export with import; they describe opposite directions of trade.

senses.definition: Still in existence; not having disappeared.
senses.example: extant manuscripts of the Old Testament

senses.definition: Still alive; not extinct.
senses.example: birds are the only extant dinosaurs

core.definition: Still in existence; surviving from the past and not lost or destroyed.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, EK. The final -ant is a weak, reduced vowel, so it sounds like 'stunt' without the t being heavy.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a precise descriptive term, often used for objects, texts, or records.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use extant in academic, historical, legal, or scientific writing, and in careful speech about surviving documents, species, or buildings. Everyday speakers prefer 'still exists' or 'survived.' Use it with things that have lasted from earlier times.

distinctions.note: Existing is common and neutral; extant is formal and often suggests survival from an earlier time.
Extinct means no longer living or no longer in use; extant means still in existence.

examples.everyday: Only a couple of copies of that old comic book are still extant, so they're worth a lot.
examples.professional: Before we start the migration, we should list all extant backups of the customer database.
examples.analytical: Scholars judge a theory by how well it accounts for the extant evidence, not by what has been lost.

nuance.analogy: Extant is like a photograph that survived a flood while the rest of the album was destroyed.
nuance.etymology: From Latin extant-, the present participle of extare, 'to stand out, be visible.'
common_mistakes: Using extant to mean 'existing now' for everything, when it suggests survival from an earlier time.
Pronouncing it with a long a in the first syllable (AYK-stunt); the first syllable is short, as in 'ex.'
patterns: extant (usually after a noun or verb)

extant.etymology: First attested in 1545, from Latin *extantem*, *extāns*, present participle of *extō* (“to stand out, exist, be extant”), from *ex-* (“out”) + *stō* (“stand”).

senses.definition: Capable of being extended.

core.definition: Able to be made longer, larger, or more extensive; capable of being extended, such as a product, cord, or contract.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on STEN, the second syllable. The final -able is weak and sounds like bul, so keep the vowels reduced and do not say it as a full ah-ble.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It describes a feature of a product, system, or contract and carries no strong emotion.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use extendable most often for products, such as extendable cords, ladders, or handles, and in software or contracts. It is the preferred spelling in American English over extendible. For general extension of time or space, people often use extended or extensible in technical writing.

distinctions.note: Extensible is more technical and often describes software or systems designed to accept added features, while extendable is the everyday physical or general word.
Extended describes something already made longer, while extendable describes something capable of being made longer.

examples.everyday: I bought an extendable ladder so I can reach the gutters without climbing on the roof.
examples.professional: Our API is extendable, so teams can add new endpoints without changing the core service.
examples.analytical: Whether a concept is extendable depends on whether its definition can be generalized consistently beyond its original domain.

nuance.analogy: Like a telescoping antenna that slides out when you need more length and folds back when you do not.
nuance.etymology: From extend, from Latin extendere 'to stretch out', plus the suffix -able 'capable of'.
common_mistakes: Spelling it extendible in American writing, where extendable is more common.
Stressing the first syllable (EKS-tend-uh-bul) instead of STEN in the middle.

senses.definition: An extroverted person: one who is outgoing, sociable, and concerned with outer affairs.
senses.example: My brother is an extrovert who loves hosting parties and meeting strangers.

senses.definition: To turn or thrust outwards.
senses.example: The engineer designed the pipe to extrovert the hot exhaust away from the building.

core.definition: A person who is outgoing, sociable, and energized by being around other people.

pronunciation.tip: The stress is on the first syllable, EK. The second syllable is a reduced "struh" and the last is "vurt," with the r clearly pronounced. Americans also accept the spelling "extravert" with the same sound.

nuance.connotation: Positive
nuance.usage_note: Americans commonly use "extrovert" to describe someone who is social and talkative, as in "She's a real extrovert." The spelling "extravert" is used by some psychologists, but "extrovert" is far more common in everyday American English. Calling someone an extrovert is a compliment or neutral description; it is not an insult.

distinctions.note: An introvert gains energy from solitude or quiet, while an extrovert gains energy from social interaction; they describe general personality tendencies, not shyness.
Outgoing describes someone friendly and easy to meet; extrovert is a broader personality term.

examples.everyday: My sister is such an extrovert; she knows everyone at the party by the end of the night.
examples.professional: During team offsites, the extroverts tend to dominate the discussion, so I make sure everyone gets a chance to speak.
examples.analytical: Jung's typology uses extroversion and introversion to describe the direction of a person's psychic energy.

nuance.analogy: Like a radio tuned to a loud station: an extrovert's energy broadcasts outward to the people around them.
nuance.etymology: Coined from Latin extra (outside) and vertere (to turn), meaning turned outward, popularized by Carl Jung.
common_mistakes: Mispronouncing the stress as "ex-TROH-vert."
Using "extrovert" as a verb in ordinary speech; the verb form is rare and sounds technical.

extrovert.etymology: Alteration of earlier *extravert* (by influence of *introvert*), from German *Extravert*, popularized in psychology by Phyllis Blanchard's 1918 "Psycho-Analytic Study of August Comte".

conversation.text: She's a total extrovert; she gets energy from being around people.
My husband is an extrovert, and I'm the one who wants to leave early.
You don't have to be an extrovert to be good at networking.

senses.definition: Very happy, especially at someone else's defeat or failure.

core.definition: Feeling or showing triumphant joy, especially after a victory or someone else's failure. Often describes a crowd, a smile or a shout.

pronunciation.tip: Stress ZUL, the second syllable. The -ant ending is reduced to 'unt', and the l is clear.

nuance.connotation: Positive when describing a team's win, but can sound smug or gloating when directed at a rival's loss.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use exultant in news reports and everyday talk about sports, elections and personal victories, such as 'the exultant crowd rushed the field'. In casual speech, 'thrilled' or 'over the moon' is more common. Be aware that describing someone as exultant at another's failure can sound mean-spirited.

distinctions.note: Elated describes great happiness in general, while exultant adds a sense of triumph, often over a win or a rival.
Exuberant describes overflowing energy and enthusiasm, while exultant focuses specifically on triumphant joy.

examples.everyday: My brother was exultant when he finally beat me at chess after twenty years.
examples.professional: The sales team was exultant after closing the contract, although the margins were thinner than we hoped.
examples.analytical: The essay criticizes the exultant tone of commentators who celebrated the rival's collapse as a moral victory.

nuance.analogy: Like a runner who throws both arms up across the finish line, exultant joy is joy that rises up and announces itself.
nuance.etymology: From Latin exsultare 'to leap up, rejoice', via exult.
common_mistakes: Confusing exultant with exuberant; exultant is about triumph, exuberant is about energy.
Misspelling it as 'exaltant', which is a different word meaning raised in rank or praise.

exultant.etymology: From Latin *exsultāns*, present participle of *exsultō* (“rejoice; boast”).

senses.definition: To communicate with somebody using the FaceTime videotelephony software.
To communicate with somebody using any form of video telephony software.
senses.example: We FaceTimed my grandmother every Sunday so she could see the kids open presents.

core.definition: To talk with someone on a video call using Apple's FaceTime app, so both people can see each other.

pronunciation.tip: Both parts get some stress, but the first syllable is stronger. Say 'face' and 'time' clearly, and do not blend them into 'fay-stime'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and friendly; it suggests a personal, casual video call with family or friends.
nuance.usage_note: FaceTime is an Apple trademark, but Americans use it generically as a verb for any video call, even on other devices. People say things like 'I'll FaceTime you tonight' or 'Let's FaceTime.' For a more general term or for work calls, Americans often say 'video call' or 'Zoom' if that is the platform used.

distinctions.note: Video call is the general term, while FaceTime names a specific app or sometimes is used generically in casual speech.
Zoom is a different company's platform, often used for work meetings, while FaceTime is more personal.

examples.everyday: Can we FaceTime tonight so I can show you the new house?
examples.professional: Let's FaceTime with the client instead of a phone call so we can review the slides together.
examples.analytical: Apps like FaceTime changed everyday communication by making the video call feel like a normal part of personal life.

nuance.analogy: Think of FaceTime as the way people in America say 'Kleenex' for a tissue: a brand name that became the everyday word.
nuance.etymology: Combines 'face' and 'time'; FaceTime was launched by Apple in 2010 as a trademark.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing it as one smooth word with no stress on the first syllable.
Saying 'FaceTime him at' with an unnecessary preposition; the verb takes a direct object: 'FaceTime him.'

facetime.etymology: Compare *face time* (“the amount of time spent in visual communication with another party”).

conversation.text: Let's FaceTime tonight so the kids can see Grandma.
I FaceTimed my brother to show him the new apartment.
She's on FaceTime with her mom; give her a minute.

senses.definition: That does not cause undue damage in the event of failure.
senses.example: The system is failsafe, because everything is backed up automatically.

senses.definition: Designed to shut off for safety if an emergency occurs.
senses.example: The reactor's cooling valve is fail-safe, closing automatically if power is lost.

senses.definition: A device, mechanism or measure designed to make something fail-safe.
senses.example: The engineers added a fail-safe that stops the elevator when the cable slackens.

senses.definition: To compensate automatically, in the event of a failure.
senses.example: When one node goes down, the network fail-safes by rerouting traffic to a backup.

senses.definition: To make a device or mechanism fail-safe, or to add a fail-safe device or mechanism to an existing system.
senses.example: Our team plans to fail-safe the old pump controller before the summer shutdown.

core.definition: Designed so that a malfunction does not cause harm, usually by shutting off or defaulting to a safe state.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on 'safe', the second word, not on 'fail'. Keep the 'l' in 'fail' clear and avoid stressing both words equally.

nuance.connotation: Positive. It describes careful design that protects people and property, though it can imply that a system was built to expect failure.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'fail-safe' in engineering, safety regulation, business and everyday talk about products such as garage doors, elevators and alarms. It is written with a hyphen when used before a noun. In casual speech, people sometimes say 'it's foolproof', but 'foolproof' means no errors can happen, while 'fail-safe' accepts that errors happen and limits their damage.

distinctions.note: 'Foolproof' means something is so simple that it cannot go wrong, while 'fail-safe' accepts that failure can occur but limits its harm.
'Redundant' means having a backup, while 'fail-safe' means the design ensures a safe result when something breaks, which may not require a backup.
'Reliable' describes how often something works, while 'fail-safe' describes what happens when it stops working.

examples.everyday: My garage door is fail-safe, so if something blocks it on the way down, it reverses instead of crushing anything.
examples.professional: The new payment gateway is fail-safe: if the connection drops mid-transaction, it rejects the charge rather than billing the customer twice.
examples.analytical: A fail-safe design forces the designer to ask what a system should do when it can no longer fulfill its purpose, which is an ethical question as well as a technical one.

nuance.analogy: A fail-safe is like a circuit breaker: when something goes wrong, it cuts the power before the house catches fire.
nuance.etymology: Compound of 'fail' and 'safe'; the term came into engineering use in the twentieth century.
common_mistakes: Stressing 'fail' rather than 'safe', which sounds unnatural to American speakers.
Omitting the hyphen before a noun, as in 'a fail safe design', which is less standard in American writing.

senses.definition: To fail, especially in a dramatic or particularly decisive manner.

core.definition: To fail badly, especially in a dramatic or embarrassing way that people notice.

pronunciation.tip: Stress face, which has the long a of say. The word one's is a weak, quick possessive, sounding like wunz, so keep it unstressed and linked smoothly.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It describes a visible failure and is often used with humor or sympathy.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say fall on your face in casual conversation about a performance, plan, or joke that fails badly. In everyday speech the possessive usually changes to match the speaker, as in fall on your face or fall on our faces, so 'one's' is mainly a dictionary form. It is informal, so do not use it in formal reports. A natural reply is 'Well, at least you tried.'

distinctions.note: Fall flat is about failing to get a reaction, while fall on your face implies a more visible and dramatic failure.
Blow it is informal for making a mistake or losing an opportunity, and it is less vivid than fall on your face.

collocations: fall on your face in public
fall on their faces during the demo

examples.everyday: She promised to cook for twenty people, and she really fell on her face.
examples.professional: If the demo fails in front of the executives, we're going to fall on our faces.
examples.analytical: A theory that predicts too much is likely to fall on its face when it confronts the data.

nuance.analogy: Like a runner who trips at the finish line in front of the crowd.
nuance.etymology: Fall comes from Old English feallan; face comes from Old French face, from Latin facies.
common_mistakes: Using fall on one's face literally, when the idiom means failing badly.
Forgetting that the pronoun changes with the subject, as in I fell on my face, not I fell on one's face.

senses.definition: To be less satisfactory than expected; to be inadequate or insufficient.
senses.example: I did my best, but fell far short of the score cutoff.

core.definition: To fail to reach a goal, standard or expectation, or to be less satisfactory than hoped for.

pronunciation.tip: In this phrasal verb the particle short takes the main stress, so say it clearly rather than letting it fade. The vowel is the open o of cot and caught, and the r is pronounced clearly in American speech.

nuance.connotation: Negative but mild: it criticizes a result without accusing anyone of total failure. Stronger words like fail sound harsher.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this in work reviews, product reviews, sports talk and everyday complaints, as in 'The movie fell short of the book.' It is polite enough for meetings. A natural reply is 'Yeah, it didn't quite measure up,' or 'You're right, we fell short.' When you give the target, always follow it with of.

distinctions.note: Fail means not succeeding at all and sounds harsher; fall short suggests you came close but did not reach the target.
Miss is usually about one specific target or chance; fall short describes an overall result below a standard or expectation.

collocations: fall short of what we need
fall short by a few points

examples.everyday: The burger was tasty, but the fries fell short of what I was hoping for.
examples.professional: Q3 sales fell short of forecast by about six percent, so we need to revisit the pipeline assumptions.
examples.analytical: Many accounts of justice fall short of explaining what we owe to people who can never repay us.

nuance.analogy: Like a free throw that hits the rim: close, but not in.
nuance.etymology: Fall from Old English feallan 'to drop'; short from Old English sceort 'brief, not long'.
common_mistakes: Saying 'fall short to' instead of 'fall short of'.
Using it for something that is simply bad; it means not reaching an expected level, so it implies a gap.

senses.definition: One who falls.
senses.example: As a faller on the ice, she learned to tuck her elbows and roll.

senses.definition: A fruit that falls from the tree, rather than being picked.
A part which acts by falling, such as a stamp in a fulling mill, or the device in a spinning machine to arrest motion when a thread breaks.
senses.example: The mill's fallers lifted and dropped the heavy stamps to felt the cloth.

senses.definition: Synonym of feller (“one who cuts down trees”).
senses.example: The logging crew hired a faller to take down the diseased oaks.

core.definition: Something, especially fruit, that has fallen from a tree rather than being picked.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable and end with an American r-colored vowel, not a hard uh sound. Keep the l clear and do not make the word sound like falter.

nuance.connotation: Neutral: it is a descriptive term for fruit or a mechanical part.
nuance.usage_note: Americans rarely use faller in daily speech. It appears mostly in agriculture, cider making and mechanical or textile contexts. In everyday English, people more often say windfall for fruit that falls from the tree or simply fallen apples.

distinctions.note: A windfall is fruit blown down by wind, or an unexpected gain; faller is a neutral technical term for any fruit that drops.
Picked fruit is harvested by hand and is often sold for eating, while fallers are often used for cider or processing.

examples.everyday: We gathered the fallers from under the apple tree and made a batch of cider.
examples.professional: The orchard report excludes fallers from the top grade because they bruise more easily in storage.
examples.analytical: The distinction between fallers and picked fruit matters for quality, since the grading system treats them differently.

nuance.analogy: Like a leaf that the wind has taken down before anyone could pick it.
nuance.etymology: From the verb fall with the agent suffix -er.
common_mistakes: Using faller to mean a person who falls; the usual word is someone who falls or a person who fell.
Confusing faller with falter, which means to lose strength or hesitate.

senses.definition: Verbal noun of fall.
senses.example: Her falling behind in class worried the teachers and her parents throughout the entire semester.

core.definition: The act or process of moving downward, or of decreasing in amount, level or value.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the first syllable, FAW. Many Americans say the vowel like the 'ah' in 'father' because of the cot-caught merger, so either vowel is understood, but keep the l clear and do not add an extra vowel after it.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It describes a movement or trend without judgment, though the context can make it positive or negative.
nuance.usage_note: As a noun, falling is less common than the verb, but Americans use it in phrases like 'falling prices' or 'the falling of snow' more often than the bare noun. Everyday speech tends to use 'the fall' for an autumn season or a drop, so falling as a noun sounds a bit literary or descriptive.

distinctions.note: Fall is the more common noun for a single drop or an autumn season, while falling emphasizes the ongoing process.
Dropping implies someone or something releases an object, while falling does not need an agent.

examples.everyday: The falling temperatures tonight mean we will need our jackets.
examples.professional: The falling conversion rates in the quarterly report worried the sales team.
examples.analytical: Newton's account of the falling apple shows how ordinary observation can reveal universal laws.

nuance.analogy: Falling is like a leaf drifting from a tree: the motion is continuous and takes its own time.
nuance.etymology: From fall (Old English feallan) plus the verbal noun ending -ing.
common_mistakes: Confusing falling with felling, which means cutting down trees, though the two sound similar.
Using falling as a single event noun where 'fall' is more natural, as in 'a big fall in prices' rather than 'a big falling'.

senses.definition: Fanatical.
senses.example: His fanatic devotion to the team made him skip his cousin's wedding for a playoff game.

senses.definition: A person who is zealously enthusiastic for some cause.
senses.example: The rally drew fanatics who shouted over every speaker and refused to listen to reason.

core.definition: A person who is excessively and uncritically devoted to a cause, belief or activity.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the second syllable, NAT. The first vowel is a weak schwa, and the final '-ic' is pronounced 'ik', not 'eek'.

nuance.connotation: Negative when describing serious beliefs; playful when describing hobbies, as in 'a coffee fanatic'.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say 'a fitness fanatic' or 'a coffee fanatic' in a playful way. 'Religious fanatic' or 'political fanatic' is serious and insulting. The word is also an adjective, as in 'fanatic believers', but the noun is more common.

distinctions.note: A fan admires something enthusiastically; a fanatic's enthusiasm is extreme and often unreasonable.
A zealot is driven by religious or political conviction, often toward uncompromising action; fanatic is broader.

examples.everyday: My brother is a coffee fanatic; he weighs his beans every morning.
examples.professional: Our senior engineer is a testing fanatic, so every pull request needs full coverage before it merges.
examples.analytical: Critics argue that a fanatic treats one principle as the only measure of truth, excluding the evidence that might correct it.

nuance.analogy: A fanatic is like a runner who has lost sight of the finish line and keeps circling the track faster and faster.
nuance.etymology: From Latin fanaticus, meaning frenzied or inspired by a god, from fanum, temple.
common_mistakes: Stressing the wrong syllable, as in FAN-uh-tik.
Calling someone a fanatic as a compliment in a serious context, which can offend.

senses.definition: Having a fat tail; leptokurtic.

core.definition: Describing a probability distribution whose tails decay more slowly than a normal distribution, so extreme values are more likely.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on TAILD, the second word. Keep the d in tailed clear, and do not reduce the vowel in fat.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and technical; in risk discussions it may signal danger from rare but severe events.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use fat-tailed mainly in statistics, finance and risk management, often with a clear sense of its technical meaning. In general conversation, people would rarely use it. When describing extreme events, data scientists may also say 'heavy-tailed,' which is nearly synonymous in most contexts.

distinctions.note: Heavy-tailed is a broader term for distributions with tails heavier than an exponential; fat-tailed is common in finance and risk and is often used interchangeably.
A normal distribution has thin tails; fat-tailed distributions give extreme outcomes much higher probability.

examples.everyday: My finance friend says the market is fat-tailed, which means crashes happen more often than people expect.
examples.professional: We switched to a fat-tailed model for the loss estimates because the Gaussian fit underestimates extreme claims.
examples.analytical: A fat-tailed distribution challenges the assumptions behind classical risk measures, since its moments may not exist.

nuance.analogy: Like a river that usually flows gently but occasionally floods far beyond its banks.
nuance.etymology: Compound of fat and tailed, describing the thick tail of a probability curve.
common_mistakes: Saying 'fat tail' without the hyphen when used as an adjective before a noun.
Assuming fat-tailed means a distribution is bigger or more common in the middle.

senses.definition: A branching, hair-like structure that grows on the bodies of birds, used for flight, swimming, protection and display.
senses.example: The hawk's brown feather drifted down onto the trail beside our tent.

senses.definition: Long hair on the lower legs of a dog or horse, especially a draft horse, notably the Clydesdale breed. Narrowly only the rear hair.
senses.example: The Clydesdale's long feather was brushed and combed before the parade.

senses.definition: One of the fins or wings on the shaft of an arrow.
senses.example: The fletcher trimmed each feather on the arrow to exactly the same length.

senses.definition: A longitudinal strip projecting from an object to strengthen it, or to enter a channel in another object and thereby prevent displacement sideways or rotationally but permit motion lengthwise.
senses.example: The machinist fitted a feather into the steel plate so the slide couldn't twist sideways.

senses.definition: Kind; nature; species (from the proverbial phrase "birds of a feather").
senses.example: Birds of a feather flock together, so the hiring committee favored candidates like themselves.

senses.definition: One of the two shims of the three-piece stone-splitting tool known as plug and feather or plug and feathers; the feathers are placed in a borehole and then a wedge is driven between them, causing the stone to split.
senses.example: The quarry crew set the feathers in the borehole and drove the wedge between them.

senses.definition: The angular adjustment of an oar or paddle-wheel float, with reference to a horizontal axis, as it leaves or enters the water.
senses.example: Good crew coaches measure each rower's feather angle as the blade leaves the water.

senses.definition: Anything petty or trifling; a whit or jot.
senses.example: She didn't care a feather what the neighbors thought about her new hairstyle.

senses.definition: Partridges and pheasants, as opposed to rabbits and hares (called fur).
senses.example: Hunters in our club bag more feather than fur in the autumn season.

senses.definition: A junction indicator attached to a color-light signal at an angle, which lights up, typically with four white lights in a row, when a diverging route is set up.
senses.example: The signal gantry's feather lit up, showing the train would take the diverging route.

senses.definition: A faint edge.
senses.example: A feather of light showed along the edge of the closed door.

senses.definition: To cover or furnish with feathers; to fletch.
senses.example: She spent the evening feathering arrows for the archery club's spring tournament.

senses.definition: To adorn, as if with feathers; to fringe.
senses.example: Her winter hat was feathered with soft fringe that brushed her cheeks.

senses.definition: To arrange in the manner or appearance of feathers.
senses.example: The stylist feathered my hair.

senses.definition: To rotate the oars while they are out of the water to reduce wind resistance.
senses.example: Between strokes, the rowers feather their oars to cut wind resistance on the return.

senses.definition: To streamline the blades of an aircraft's propeller by rotating them perpendicular to the axis of the propeller when the engine is shut down so that the propeller does not windmill during flight.
senses.example: After striking the bird, the pilot feathered the damaged left engine’s propeller.

senses.definition: To finely shave or bevel an edge.
senses.example: He carefully feathered the edge of the tin sheet with a fine file.

senses.definition: To intergrade or blend the pixels of an image with those of a background or neighboring image.
senses.example: The editor feathered the edges of the pasted sky so it blended into the background.

senses.definition: Of written or printed ink: to take on a blurry appearance as a result of spreading through the receiving medium.
To render light as a feather; to give wings to.
To enrich; to exalt; to benefit.
To tread, as a cockerel.
To move the cue back and forth along the bridge in preparation for striking the cue ball.
To accidentally touch the cue ball with the tip of the cue when taking aim.
To touch lightly, like (or as if with) a feather.
To move softly, like a feather.

core.definition: One of the light, soft, branching structures that cover a bird's body and help it fly and stay warm.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable. The th is voiced, as in this, not unvoiced as in think, and the final -er is a reduced r-colored vowel, not a long e.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive. Light as a feather suggests gentleness and ease, while ruffling someone's feathers suggests annoyance.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use feather in everyday talk about birds, pillows, hats, and decorations. Idioms like birds of a feather and ruffle someone's feathers are common in casual speech. As a verb, feather is less common and sounds craft-related or technical.

distinctions.note: A plume is a large, showy feather or group of feathers, often for decoration; feather is the general word.
Down is the soft, fluffy under-feathering used in pillows and jackets; a feather has a firm central shaft.

examples.everyday: I found a blue feather in the backyard after the crows were fighting.
examples.professional: The new prototype weighs almost nothing, as light as a feather, so our shipping costs should drop.
examples.analytical: Ezekiel's imagery of wings and feathers reflects the ancient link between covering and protection.

nuance.analogy: A feather's branching barbs lock together like Velcro, which is why a bird can smooth them back into place.
nuance.etymology: From Old English fether, from Proto-Germanic fethro, related to Latin penna and Greek pteron.
common_mistakes: Using feather as an uncountable noun; say a feather or feathers.
Pronouncing th as a t sound, as in fether with a hard t.
nuance.biblical_note: Feathers appear in Scripture mainly through images of wings and covering. The Hebrew word kanaph means wing, edge, or extremity, and the image of God covering His people with wings expresses protection. Psalm 91:4 describes God sheltering the faithful under His pinions and wings. Matthew 23:37 and Luke 13:34 compare Jesus' desire to gather Jerusalem to a hen gathering her brood under her wings.

feather.etymology: From Middle English *fethere*, from Old English *feþer*, from **feþru*, from Proto-Germanic **feþrō*, from Proto-Indo-European **péth₂r̥* (“feather, wing”), from **peth₂-* (“to fly”).

senses.definition: A person who fells trees; a lumberjack.
A machine for felling trees.
A person who fells a seam.
senses.example: The skilled feller finished the sleeve seams so neatly that they lay flat against the cloth.

senses.definition: An appliance to a sewing machine for felling a seam.
senses.example: Attach the feller to the machine before sewing the flat-felled seam on the denim jeans.

core.definition: A worker who cuts down trees for lumber, or a machine that does this work.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable and pronounce the second syllable as a weak, reduced 'er' sound, not a full 'ay' or 'ah.' Learners often make it sound like two separate words, 'fell' and 'ur.'

nuance.connotation: Neutral and descriptive. It describes a job rather than a personality.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'feller' in forestry, logging, and timber work. In everyday speech, most people say 'logger' or 'lumberjack' instead. Do not confuse this with the informal spoken word 'feller,' meaning 'fellow' or 'guy,' which is a dialect spelling.

distinctions.note: A logger often does the whole process, including felling, limbing, and hauling logs. A feller only cuts down the trees.
Lumberjack is a popular, folksy term for a logger and is more common in stories and advertising than in the industry.
An arborist cares for trees, trims them, and removes them safely in towns. A feller works in forestry and timber harvesting.

examples.everyday: My uncle worked as a feller in Oregon for twenty years before his back gave out.
examples.professional: The contractor hired two experienced fellers and a skidder crew to start the harvest on Monday.
examples.analytical: The feller's judgment about the lean of a trunk determined the safety of the entire crew, since a misread tree can fall the wrong way.

nuance.analogy: The feller is like the surgeon who makes the first cut: the opening action that determines everything that comes after.
nuance.etymology: From the verb 'fell' (from Old English fellan, 'to cause to fall') plus the suffix '-er.'
common_mistakes: Confusing 'feller' with 'fellow' in writing, since the spoken forms are similar.
Pronouncing it as two full syllables, 'FELL-ur,' instead of a reduced second syllable.

senses.definition: An intense, heated emotion; passion, ardor.
senses.example: The coach trains his water polo team with fervor.

senses.definition: A passionate enthusiasm for some cause.
Heat.
senses.example: Under the fervor of the July sun, the old preacher wiped his brow and kept on preaching.

core.definition: Intense, passionate feeling or enthusiasm for a cause, belief, or activity.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable. The final syllable is an unstressed r-colored vowel, so say it as 'er' with the tongue curled, not as 'or'.

nuance.connotation: Positive or neutral when describing devotion or energy; it can turn negative when it suggests reckless extremism or mob emotion.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use fervor in news, speeches, politics, religion, and business writing, often with words like religious, patriotic, or campaign. In casual talk people more often say enthusiasm or excitement. The British spelling is fervour, so American writing should use fervor.

distinctions.note: Enthusiasm is the everyday word for interest and eagerness; fervor implies deeper, more intense passion that can border on zeal.
Zeal is stronger and often suggests dedication to a goal or religious cause, while fervor can describe feelings in general.
Ardor is more romantic or poetic and often refers to love or desire, while fervor is used more for causes, beliefs, or public feeling.

examples.everyday: The kids got into a fervor about the science fair, and they barely slept all week.
examples.professional: The team's fervor for the migration project was impressive, but we need to slow down and test the data pipeline first.
examples.analytical: Historians have long debated whether the religious fervor of the revival was a cause or a symptom of social change.

nuance.analogy: Fervor is like a fire that burns brightly in the heart; it gives warmth and energy, but unchecked it can spread out of control.
nuance.etymology: From Latin fervor, 'heat, glow,' from fervere, 'to boil'.
common_mistakes: Spelling it fervour, the British form; use fervor in American writing.
Saying with a fervor for something is fine, but many learners wrongly use in fervor instead of with fervor.

fervor.etymology: From Middle English *fervour*, from Old French, from Latin *fervor* (“a boiling or raging heat, heat, vehemence, passion”), from *fervere* (“to boil, be hot”); see fervent.

senses.definition: Having the atmosphere, decoration, or attitude of a festival, holiday, or celebration.
senses.example: The room was decked out in festive streamers, with flowers everywhere.

senses.definition: In the mood to celebrate.
senses.example: Please put the Christmas decorations away, I'm really not in a festive mood.

core.definition: Cheerful, joyful, and celebratory, especially as at a holiday, party, or festival.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable. The second syllable is a short 'ih', so say it as 'FES-tiv', not 'FES-teev'.

nuance.connotation: Positive; it suggests cheerfulness and holiday spirit.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use festive all the time for holidays, parties, decorations, and gatherings, such as festive lights or a festive mood. You can describe a person as in a festive mood. It is friendly and casual, and it works well in both speech and writing.

distinctions.note: Festal is more formal and literary, while festive is the everyday word for celebratory atmosphere.
Cheerful describes a general happy mood, while festive describes a celebration or holiday atmosphere.

examples.everyday: The whole office looked festive with lights and paper garlands before the holiday party.
examples.professional: The team kept a festive tone at the launch party, but everyone was still checking the dashboard.
examples.analytical: The essay argues that the festive rituals of the medieval church blended joy with penitence in complex ways.

nuance.analogy: A festive room is like a bright sweater on a cold day: it lifts the mood and makes everyone want to join in.
nuance.etymology: From Latin festivus, 'of a feast,' from festum, 'feast'.
common_mistakes: Confusing festive with festival, the noun for the event itself.
Saying festive person when you mean a cheerful person; use festive for atmosphere or events more than for character.

festive.etymology: From French *festif*, from Latin *festivus* (“pertaining to a feast, gay, lively, joyous”).

senses.definition: Characteristic of feuilletonism.

core.definition: Relating to or characteristic of feuilletons or feuilletonism, that is, light, witty, topical writing printed in newspapers.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the syllable before -istic, which is NIS, as in 'realistic'. Do not stress the TAH from feuilleton, and keep the final -ic as a short 'ik'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to mildly dismissive; it can suggest breezy, superficial cultural writing rather than rigorous argument.
nuance.usage_note: Critics and literary historians use this word, but it rarely appears in speech. Americans would more often call a piece magazine-style or chatty, though feuilletonistic is the precise literary term for that quality.

distinctions.note: Journalistic means reporting news in general; feuilletonistic describes the lighter, essayistic, cultural style of a newspaper feature.
Essayistic is broader and more reflective; feuilletonistic points to brevity, wit and topicality in a newspaper setting.

examples.professional: The draft is too feuilletonistic for a technical report, so we need evidence and data rather than anecdotes.
examples.analytical: Some early twentieth-century essays are feuilletonistic in form, yet they hide a rigorous analysis of modern urban life.

nuance.analogy: A feuilletonistic piece is like a well-made pastry: small, crisp and stylish, not a full meal.
nuance.etymology: Formed from feuilleton, the French newspaper feature, plus the suffix -istic, meaning characteristic of.
common_mistakes: Stressing the TAH syllable from feuilleton instead of the NIS syllable.
Using it to mean simply 'journalistic' or 'fictional', when it refers to a light, cultural newspaper style.

senses.definition: Calculation.
Structure, design, or arrangement; figure.
senses.example: The intricate figuring on the silk scarf caught the afternoon light beautifully.

senses.definition: Representation.
senses.example: Her essay questioned the figuring of women in medieval romance.

core.definition: The act or result of calculating or working out a number or amount, often an estimate.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable. The -ure in figure becomes a weak yer sound, and the ending is -ing, with no t or g after the ng.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it describes working out numbers, and it is often used loosely for a rough estimate.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say figuring mostly in casual talk about money or planning, as in 'by my figuring, we can afford it'. In formal writing they would use calculation or estimate. It is most common in the phrase 'my figuring' or 'rough figuring'.

distinctions.note: Calculation is more formal and precise, while figuring is casual and often refers to a rough mental or informal working out.
An estimate is an approximate judgment of value, while figuring is the process of working out numbers, which may lead to an estimate.

examples.everyday: By my figuring, we can split the dinner bill four ways and still tip well.
examples.professional: The budget figuring in the spreadsheet looks right, but please double-check the tax assumptions.
examples.analytical: His figuring of the probabilities assumed independence, which the data do not support.

nuance.analogy: Figuring is like doing sums on the back of an envelope: it is a quick, practical way to reach a number.
nuance.etymology: From figure, from Latin figura 'shape, form', with the -ing suffix.
common_mistakes: Using figuring for the whole result; in careful writing, figure or calculation may be better.
Confusing the noun figuring with the verb phrase 'I'm figuring', which means 'I think'.

senses.definition: Eat so much of one thing that you have no room for the rest.

core.definition: To eat so much of one food that you have little or no room left for other foods.

pronunciation.tip: "Up" is reduced to a weak "uhp" and the stress lands on "on," which is pronounced with the open American "ah" vowel. Link "fill up on" smoothly so it sounds like "fil-uh-PAHN."

nuance.connotation: Mildly negative when used as advice against eating too much of something filling but unhealthy, such as bread or chips.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say this at restaurants and dinner tables when someone eats too much bread or chips before the meal: "Don't fill up on bread." A natural reply is "Yeah, I'll pace myself." It is casual and everyday, not used for formal writing.

distinctions.note: "Stuff yourself" means eating a lot quickly and is more strongly negative than "fill up on".
"Snack on" means eating small amounts casually between meals, while "fill up on" implies eating enough to block appetite.

examples.everyday: Don't fill up on chips before the entrées come out.
examples.professional: If the team fills up on quick wins, nobody will want to tackle the hard infrastructure work.
examples.analytical: Consumers who fill up on cheap calories may fail to get the nutrients their bodies need.

nuance.analogy: Like pouring a glass of water before the main course, so the meal you came for barely fits.
nuance.etymology: A phrasal verb from "fill," "up" and "on"; no separate root.
common_mistakes: Saying "fill on" without "up".
Using "fill up with" in this sense; "fill up on" is the idiom for food.
Stressing "up" instead of "on".

conversation.text: Don't fill up on chips before dinner.
The kids filled up on bread and didn't eat their meals.
I filled up on salad, so I skipped dessert.

senses.definition: Synonym of last straw.
senses.example: Her boss's rude comment about her report was the final straw, and she quit that afternoon.

core.definition: The last problem or annoyance that makes someone's patience finally break, after earlier troubles have built up.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on STRAW, the last word, and final is lighter. Pronounce the l in final as a syllabic sound, 'fine-uhl', and the vowel in straw as in 'law', with the r pronounced.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It expresses frustration, exhaustion or the point where someone stops tolerating a situation.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say final straw when a series of problems finally causes someone to react, often with a sigh or a dramatic tone. For example, after a broken printer and a late delivery, someone might say 'That's the final straw!' A natural reply is 'Yeah, I'd be upset too.' It is informal, so avoid it in serious formal complaints where breaking point or a direct statement fits better.

distinctions.note: Last straw is the more familiar idiom; final straw means the same thing and both are used in American speech.
Breaking point is the moment of collapse itself, which comes after the final straw.
Tipping point describes when a gradual change becomes irreversible, often in business or social issues, not personal frustration.

collocations: a series of problems leading to the final straw

examples.everyday: The dishwasher broke, the car needs repairs, and now the furnace is out. That's the final straw!
examples.professional: After the third missed deadline in a month, my manager said the vendor's delays were the final straw and we would switch providers.
examples.analytical: For many citizens, the final straw was not the policy itself but the sense that no one in power was listening.

nuance.analogy: Like the one extra feather that finally breaks the camel's back: the last weight added, after many smaller ones.
nuance.etymology: From the proverb about a straw breaking a camel's back, with final marking the last weight added.
common_mistakes: Using final straw for a single small irritation; the idiom needs a series of earlier problems first.
Mispronouncing the first word as 'FI-nal' with a full second vowel; it is 'fine-uhl' with a light stress.

senses.definition: The final version of a product.
Synonym of finished article.
senses.example: The brochure showed the finished product, not the rough prototype we first tested.

core.definition: The final version of a product, ready to be sold, used or delivered to a customer.

pronunciation.tip: The stress on 'product' falls on the first syllable when it is a noun, so say PRAH-duhkt, not pruh-DUKT. The first word links smoothly, so 'finished product' sounds like 'finisht PRAH-duhkt'.

nuance.connotation: Positive or neutral. It suggests something polished and ready, but in figurative use it can imply that what you see is all that has been made.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'finished product' in business, manufacturing, software and design, and also in everyday jokes, such as 'Here's the finished product' after a home project. It is a noun phrase, so say 'the finished product' rather than 'a finished product' when you mean the one final result. The phrase 'finished article' is less common in American speech and sounds slightly British or old-fashioned.

distinctions.note: 'Final product' stresses the last item in a sequence, while 'finished product' stresses that the item is complete and ready to use.
'Finished article' is a near-synonym, but Americans usually prefer 'finished product' in business and everyday speech.

examples.everyday: After three months of knitting, that sweater is the finished product, and I'm proud of it.
examples.professional: QA will test the finished product on three devices before we ship it to customers.
examples.analytical: Theory is rarely a finished product of inquiry; it is more like a scaffold that supports further investigation.

nuance.analogy: Like a loaf of bread that comes out of the oven, cooled and sliced, ready for the table.
nuance.etymology: 'Finished' comes from 'finish', from Latin finire, 'to end'; 'product' comes from Latin productum, 'something brought forth'.
common_mistakes: Stressing 'product' on the second syllable as a noun.
Saying 'a finished product' when speaking about the final version of one specific item, instead of 'the finished product'.
Using 'finished product' for a product that is still being developed.

senses.definition: An organized practice to prepare occupants of an office, school or other public building for evacuation in the event of a fire.
senses.example: There was a fire drill this morning. We had to leave the building calmly and go to the birch tree, our meeting point.

senses.definition: Any pointless, unproductive, useless, or chaotic activity.
senses.example: Since they've changed the standards again, our previous efforts now just amount to a fire drill.

senses.definition: A fire-starting tool consisting of a wooden rod and some primitive means of rapidly rotating the rod on a flat surface like a drill until tinder can be ignited.
senses.example: Using a fire drill made of cedar, he rubbed the spindle until a flame caught in the tinder.

core.definition: A planned practice in which people leave a building quickly and safely, as if there were a real fire.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on drill, and the first syllable fire is weaker, though still clear. Americans make the dr sound with a slight r-like quality, and the vowel in drill is short, as in 'bill'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it can sound playful when someone says it is a fire drill in a chaotic situation.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use fire drill for schools, offices and apartment buildings, where people practice evacuating when the alarm sounds. In informal speech, a fire drill can also mean a chaotic or pointless activity, as in this meeting turned into a fire drill. Most people will understand the expression, but it is informal.

distinctions.note: An evacuation drill is a general term for leaving a building, while a fire drill specifically practices escape from a fire.
A lockdown drill practices securing a building against an intruder, while a fire drill practices leaving because of fire.

examples.everyday: The kids came home saying they had a fire drill during math class, so they were excited to tell us about it.
examples.professional: Facilities will run a fire drill on Thursday at 10 a.m., so please use the stairs and meet in the north parking lot.
examples.analytical: A fire drill reveals whether evacuation depends on knowing the procedure or on routines practiced until movement becomes automatic.

nuance.analogy: A fire drill is like a rehearsal before a play, so the actors know their moves when the real performance begins.
nuance.etymology: Fire from Old English fyr; drill from Middle Dutch drillen, to bore or train.
common_mistakes: Using fire practice, which sounds British, instead of fire drill.
Confusing a fire drill, which is a practice, with a fire extinguisher or a real emergency.

senses.definition: To provide a thing, a group, a person, or oneself with requisites.
senses.example: The city council agreed to fit out the new clinic with modern medical equipment.

core.definition: To equip or supply a place, vehicle, group, or person with what is needed, such as furniture, tools or clothing.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on OUT, with a lighter secondary stress on fit. The t in fit links into the vowel of out, so the phrase sounds like 'fi-TOUT'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It describes practical preparation and is not emotionally loaded.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use fit out mostly for setting up offices, kitchens, labs, boats or stores with equipment. Everyday speakers more often say outfit or equip, as in 'outfit the kitchen' or 'equip the lab.' Fit out is understood and common in construction and business settings.

distinctions.note: Outfit is the more common American word and can refer to clothing as well as equipment, while fit out usually refers to installing fittings or equipment in a space or vehicle.
Equip is the general word for supplying tools or skills, while fit out suggests providing the complete set of fixtures for a place or vehicle.

examples.everyday: We are going to fit out the garage with a workbench and shelves this weekend.
examples.professional: The team will fit out the new office with standing desks and video equipment before Friday.
examples.analytical: Public money was used to fit out the lab, but the proposal never explained which experiments required the new equipment.

nuance.analogy: Like outfitting a camping trip: you bring the tents, stove and lanterns so the place works from day one.
nuance.etymology: Fit, in the sense of equip, from Middle English, plus out from Old English ūt.
common_mistakes: Using fit out for clothing, where Americans say dress up or outfit, not fit out.
Forgetting that the phrase is a separable verb, so you can say 'fit the kitchen out' as well as 'fit out the kitchen'.

senses.definition: A house, property, car, or other object that needs to be fixed up or repaired, often purchased as an investment.
A potential romantic partner who may need some motivation to improve their personality or habits.
senses.example: My sister keeps dating fixer-uppers, convinced she can change them into better partners.

senses.definition: A person who tinkers or fixes things up; in particular, someone who fixes up houses, properties, etc. as an investment.
senses.example: He buys fixer-upper houses in Ohio, renovates them, and sells them within a year.

core.definition: A house, car, or other property that needs repairs or renovation, often bought cheaply as an investment.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress is on UP, with a lighter secondary stress on FIX. The final -er in both words is a light, rhotic 'ur,' so the word has four syllables with its heaviest beat on the second half.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to mildly negative, implying work and expense; in romantic contexts, it is often joking and can sound slightly unkind.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use fixer-upper constantly in real estate, especially for a house that needs work but has potential. It is also used for a used car or old furniture. Calling a person a fixer-upper is informal and can sound unkind, so use it only jokingly. A natural reply is 'Yeah, it needs some work, but the location is great.'

distinctions.note: A handyman special is a real estate listing term for a property sold as is, usually in poor condition; a fixer-upper is any home that needs work, whether or not it is sold as is.

examples.everyday: We bought a fixer-upper with a crooked porch, but the backyard is great for the kids.
examples.professional: The firm specializes in buying fixer-upper properties, renovating them, and reselling them within six months.
examples.analytical: The fixer-upper is a useful figure for thinking about how value depends on the gap between present condition and potential.

nuance.analogy: Like an old piano at a yard sale: it needs tuning, new strings, and some love, but it can sound beautiful again.
nuance.etymology: Formed from the verb phrase fix up plus the agent suffix -er, meaning one who fixes up.
common_mistakes: Writing 'fixer upper' without a hyphen when it is used as a noun; the standard form is fixer-upper.
Stressing only the second syllable; say FIX-er-UP-er with the main stress on UP.

fixer-upper.etymology: From a reduplicating suffixation of *fix up*, equivalent to *fix* + *-er* + *up* + *-er*.

senses.definition: Flavoring, a substance used to produce a taste.
senses.example: Flavor was added to the pudding.

senses.definition: A variety (of taste) attributed to an object (food, candy, chewing gum, medicine, etc).
senses.example: What flavor of bubble gum do you most enjoy?

senses.definition: The characteristic quality of something.
senses.example: the flavor of an experience

senses.definition: A kind or type.
senses.example: Debian is one flavor of the Linux operating system.

senses.definition: Style.
senses.example: The old bungalow has a cozy flavor that the new condos completely lack.

senses.definition: One of the six types of quarks (top, bottom, strange, charmed, up, and down) or three types of leptons (electron, muon, and tauon).
senses.example: Physicists observed that the top quark has a flavor distinct from the charm quark.

senses.definition: To add flavoring to something.
senses.example: She flavored the soup with lemon zest, fresh thyme, and a pinch of salt.

core.definition: The taste of food or drink, or a substance added to create a particular taste.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, and end with a weak, reduced 'er' sound that is typical of American English. The final syllable is not 'vor' or 'vay,' and the r is pronounced in General American speech.

nuance.connotation: Positive or neutral. Describing food as having good flavor is a compliment, while a lack of flavor is a criticism.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'flavor' constantly for food, drinks, candy, and ice cream, as in 'What flavor is it?' The British spelling 'flavour' should be avoided in American writing. For a flavor in the abstract sense, Americans often say 'the flavor of the season' or 'a different flavor.'

distinctions.note: 'Taste' is the sensation on your tongue, while 'flavor' is the overall combination of taste and smell that makes food distinctive.
'Flavoring' is the substance added to food, such as vanilla or lemon extract, while 'flavor' is the resulting quality you experience.

examples.everyday: This chili has a smoky flavor, so you probably don't need extra hot sauce.
examples.professional: We're launching a new mint flavor for the product line next quarter.
examples.analytical: The flavor of a dish is more than the sum of its ingredients, since memory and expectation also shape how we taste it.

nuance.analogy: Taste is the single note you hear, while flavor is the whole chord that the food plays.
nuance.etymology: From Middle English flavour, probably from Old French flaor, meaning smell or taste.
common_mistakes: Using the British spelling 'flavour' in American writing
Pronouncing it as two syllables with a long 'o' sound at the end

flavor.etymology: From Middle English *flavour* meaning “smell, odour”, usually pleasing, borrowed from Old French *flaour* (“smell, odour”), from Vulgar Latin **flātor* (“odour, that which blows”), from Latin *flātor* (“blower”), from *flo* (“to blow, puff”), ultimately…

conversation.text: What flavor of ice cream do you want?
The soup doesn't have much flavor.
Fresh herbs add a lot of flavor.

senses.definition: Synonym of thumb (“to turn the pages of (a book) in order to read it cursorily”).
senses.example: She flipped through the novel quickly, skimming pages before deciding to buy it.

core.definition: To turn the pages of a book, magazine or similar item quickly, looking at parts of it without reading closely.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on THROO, the particle at the end. The th is voiced in 'through' only in some words, so here it is the unvoiced th sound followed by a short r, so do not say 'flip-THROO' with a hard t.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It describes casual reading, so it is not a criticism unless someone is skimming when you expected careful reading.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this for magazines, catalogs, menus, documents and phone or TV channels: 'I was flipping through channels for an hour.' Used for a book it implies skimming, so do not use it to describe serious study of a text. 'Thumb through' is a close synonym in everyday speech.

distinctions.note: Skim suggests reading quickly for the main points; flip through suggests turning pages with less focus, often just looking at pictures or headings.
Browse is more relaxed and can mean choosing or exploring, especially in stores or online; flip through is closer to physically turning pages.

examples.everyday: I was just flipping through a magazine while I waited for my haircut.
examples.professional: Before the meeting, flip through the slides so you know where the key numbers are.
examples.analytical: Readers often flip through a dense monograph before deciding whether to read it closely.

nuance.analogy: Like a card dealer running a thumb along the edge of a deck to see what is there.
common_mistakes: Using 'flip' with 'in' or 'on' instead of 'through' when describing channels or pages.
Saying 'flip the book' when you mean reading casually; 'flip through the book' is the natural phrase.

senses.definition: To whip or scourge as punishment.
To use something to extreme; to abuse.
senses.example: They flogged the idea so hard that the team stopped listening.

senses.definition: To overexploit (land), as by overgrazing, overstocking, etc.
senses.example: Decades of flogging the grasslands with too many cattle left the soil barren.

senses.definition: To beat away charcoal dust etc. using a flogger.
senses.example: Before the next shift, the worker flogged the charcoal dust from the sacks with a flogger.

senses.definition: A weblog designed to look authentic, but actually developed as part of a commercial marketing strategy to promote some product or service.
senses.example: The company's supposed fan blog turned out to be a flog run by its marketing department.

core.definition: To beat someone with a whip, stick or rod as a punishment.

pronunciation.tip: The vowel is the open ah of lot; the final g is hard, not like j. Keep the initial fl tight and do not add a vowel after the l.

nuance.connotation: Negative; it describes cruel, violent punishment.
nuance.usage_note: In the US, flog is mostly a historical or literary word for punishment by whipping. Everyday Americans would say whip or beat. In British English flog also means to sell aggressively, which Americans rarely use; they would say sell or hawk.

distinctions.note: Whip is the general term for striking with a lash; flog implies a formal or repeated beating as punishment.
Scourge is a more literary, religious term for severe whipping or affliction; flog is more concrete and often legal.

examples.everyday: Flogging was a brutal punishment, and I am glad we no longer use it.
examples.professional: Our history team is writing a report on how flogging was used as naval discipline.
examples.analytical: The text describes the prisoner being flogged before a crowd, a detail that shows how punishment functioned as public spectacle.

nuance.etymology: From Latin flagellare, to whip or scourge.
common_mistakes: Using flog to mean sell in American English; it sounds British or odd.
Confusing flog with flagellate or flagellum, which share a root but have other meanings.
nuance.biblical_note: In the RSV, Matthew 10:17 says people will flog the disciples in their synagogues, using the Greek mastigoō, to whip. Matthew 27:26 describes Jesus being scourged before he is handed over to be crucified, using the Greek phragelloō, to scourge. Such floggings were a common punishment imposed by religious and civil authorities.

flog.etymology: From Middle English **floggen* (suggested by *flogge* (“hammer, sledge”), from Old English **floggian*, a stem variant of Proto-Germanic **flukkōną* (“to beat”), itself a secondary zero-grade iterative with unetymological -u, derived from **flōkaną*.

senses.definition: A light, brief snowfall; a shower of snow.
senses.example: A brief flurry dusted the parking lot just before the morning commute.

senses.definition: A sudden and brief blast or gust; a light, temporary breeze.
senses.example: a flurry of wind

senses.definition: A shower of dust, leaves etc. brought on by a sudden gust of wind.
senses.example: A sudden gust sent a flurry of maple leaves swirling across the playground.

senses.definition: Any sudden activity; a stir.
senses.example: The day before the wedding was a flurry of preparations.

senses.definition: A snack consisting of soft ice cream mixed with small pieces of fruit, cookie crumbs, etc.
senses.example: After dinner we bought a peanut butter cookie flurry at the ice cream shop.

senses.definition: The violent spasms of a dying whale.
senses.example: Marine biologists recorded the flurry of a dying whale as its heart slowed.

senses.definition: An occurrence of something (countable instances) in large numbers, happening suddenly or in a short period of time.
senses.example: The fencer landed a flurry of hits on her opponent.

senses.definition: To agitate, bewilder, fluster.
senses.example: Don't let the angry customer flurry you; stay calm and listen to her complaint.

senses.definition: To move or fall in a flurry.
senses.example: Reporters flurried around the senator as she stepped out of the courthouse.

core.definition: A sudden, brief burst of activity, excitement or movement, such as a flurry of emails or a flurry of questions.

pronunciation.tip: The stress is on the first syllable. The vowel is a short uh, as in 'fluff,' not the long oo of 'flu.' The r is pronounced clearly in American English.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It suggests a short, busy, slightly chaotic period, and it can be neutral or mildly negative depending on context.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use flurry most often in the phrase 'a flurry of activity' or 'a flurry of emails,' meaning a sudden rush of activity that ends quickly. In winter weather reports, a flurry means a light, brief snowfall that barely covers the ground. In casual speech you might say 'there was a flurry of texts' or 'a flurry of questions after the meeting.'

distinctions.note: A rush is a fast movement or sudden demand, while a flurry is a short burst of many small, scattered actions or items.
A flurry is a light, brief fall of snow, while a snowstorm is heavier and lasts longer.
A spate is a series of similar events, often bad ones, and is more formal; a flurry is usually a lively, busy burst.

examples.everyday: After the game, there was a flurry of texts in the group chat.
examples.professional: We got a flurry of support tickets right after the release, so I am bringing in two more engineers.
examples.analytical: The journal saw a flurry of papers on the theory in the decade after it appeared, followed by near silence.

nuance.analogy: Like a sudden gust that scatters leaves across a yard and then dies down, a flurry is a brief, scattered burst of activity.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the vowel as the long oo of 'flu' instead of the short uh of 'fluff'.
Using flurry as a plain word for a crowd; it describes a burst of activity, not a group of people.

flurry.etymology: Perhaps an American English blend of *flutter* and *hurry*.

senses.definition: The act by which something is foiled; prevention of success.
senses.example: the foilings of our expectations

senses.definition: The track of game, such as deer, in the grass.
senses.example: The hunter followed the faint foiling of a deer through the tall wet grass.

senses.definition: Clipping of hydrofoiling (“the action of sustained hydrodynamic lift on hydrofoils lifting the vessel hull lifted out of the water, for sustained motion across water”).
senses.example: Modern foiling catamarans can lift their hulls out of the water and race at great speed.

senses.definition: A foil.
senses.example: The jeweler set the diamond on a bright foiling to make it sparkle.

core.definition: The act of preventing someone's plan, attempt or crime from succeeding. Used in news and formal writing.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, FOY, and keep the 'oy' diphthong. The second syllable is a quick unstressed 'ling' with a short i.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive, because the word describes stopping something harmful or unwanted. It is typically used in reports and formal descriptions rather than casual chat.
nuance.usage_note: Americans rarely use 'foiling' as a noun in casual speech; they more often say 'stopping,' 'preventing' or use the verb 'foiled.' You will see it in news and official writing about crimes, plots or attacks. A natural reply to news of it is simply 'Good thing they caught it.'

distinctions.note: 'Prevention' is a general noun for stopping things from happening, while 'foiling' is specific to defeating a particular plan or attempt that was already underway.
'Thwarting' is a close synonym but more literary; 'foiling' is more common in news and reports.

examples.everyday: The foiling of the bank robbery made the evening news, and the neighbors were talking about it all week.
examples.professional: The foiling of the cyberattack depended on automatic alerts and a rapid response from the security team.
examples.analytical: The foiling of the conspiracy revealed how fragile its coordination had been, since a single informant could unravel it.

nuance.analogy: Foiling a plan is like a goalkeeper stopping a shot just before it crosses the line: the goal is prevented at the last moment.
nuance.etymology: Verbal noun from 'foil' (to defeat or frustrate), from Old French 'fouler,' to trample.
common_mistakes: Using 'foiling' as a verb in a sentence; in English you say 'they foiled the plan,' not 'they foiling the plan.'
Confusing 'foiling' with 'failing'; 'foiling' means someone deliberately stopped something, not that it failed on its own.

senses.definition: (dated) A vain man; a dandy.
senses.label: dated

core.definition: A vain man who is overly concerned with fashion and his appearance; a dandy.

pronunciation.tip: Use the vowel of father, not the rounded vowel of fought, because most Americans have merged these sounds. End with a crisp p.

nuance.connotation: Negative and mocking. It suggests vanity and excessive attention to clothes.
nuance.usage_note: Fop is rare in modern American speech and sounds old-fashioned or literary, often used about 18th-century or Restoration-era characters. Americans would more likely say dandy, or the informal clotheshorse for someone who loves stylish clothes. Calling a coworker a fop would sound insulting and dated.

distinctions.note: A dandy is a man who cares a great deal about elegant clothing; fop is harsher and suggests silliness and vanity.
Clotheshorse is informal and modern American slang for someone who loves clothes; it is less insulting than fop.

examples.professional: Don't show up to the client meeting dressed like a fop; they care about the analysis, not your jacket.
examples.analytical: Restoration comedy often mocks the fop as a figure of vanity who hides a lack of substance.

nuance.analogy: A fop is like a peacock: much display, little substance.
nuance.etymology: Of uncertain origin; first recorded in English in the 1500s, apparently meaning a fool.
common_mistakes: Saying fop with the vowel of fought instead of father
Using fop as a casual compliment for someone well dressed

fop.etymology: From Middle English *foppe*, *fobbe* (“fop, fool”), but its origin is.

senses.definition: At this time.

core.definition: At this time; for now, though the situation may change later.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on MOH, the first syllable of moment. 'The' before a consonant-initial word is reduced to thuh, and the final syllable is weak, so it is MOH-muhnt, not MOH-ment.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it signals that a situation or decision is temporary.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say 'for the moment' to indicate something is temporary: 'For the moment, let's stick with the plan.' It is common in both speech and meetings. Compare 'at the moment', which describes what is happening now; 'for the moment' often hints that the situation may change.

distinctions.note: 'At the moment' describes what is true now; 'for the moment' implies the state is temporary and may change.
Very close in meaning; 'for now' is more casual and often sounds more final about a temporary plan.

examples.everyday: I'm out of cash for the moment, so can we pay by card?
examples.professional: For the moment, we'll keep the old API running while the new one is tested.
examples.analytical: For the moment, the evidence supports the hypothesis, but a larger sample could change the conclusion.

nuance.analogy: A bridge held up with temporary supports: it works now, though it is not the final design.
nuance.etymology: 'Moment' comes from Latin momentum, 'movement, importance', and later 'brief time'; this phrase uses the sense 'present time'.
common_mistakes: Confusing 'momentarily' with 'in a moment': in American English 'momentarily' usually means 'for a short time', while 'in a moment' means 'soon'.
Using 'for the moment' when you mean an action is happening right now; 'right now' or 'at the moment' fits better there.

senses.definition: To renounce or deny something, especially under oath.
senses.example: We forswear allegiance and support for the Economic Freedom Fighters.

senses.definition: To commit perjury; to break an oath.
senses.example: He swore on the Bible in court, then forswore himself when the documents proved otherwise.

core.definition: To solemnly renounce or deny something, or to swear off a practice or belief, especially under oath.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the second syllable, SWAIR, and the w is pronounced clearly. Keep the r rhotic in the final syllable, which sounds like 'air'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to negative. It can describe a serious renunciation, but when it means breaking an oath, it implies dishonor.
nuance.usage_note: Americans rarely use forswear in ordinary speech. You will hear it in legal, religious, or historical contexts, or in phrases like 'forswear alcohol'. In casual talk, say give up, swear off, or quit. Note that forswear can mean breaking an oath, which is the opposite of keeping a promise.

distinctions.note: Renounce is more formal and often refers to a public statement of rejection, such as renouncing a claim. Forswear stresses swearing an oath to stop.
Swear off is informal and everyday, as in 'swear off sweets'. Forswear is more formal and solemn.

examples.everyday: After the holidays, my brother swore he would forswear sweets, but he was back at the bakery by Friday.
examples.professional: The contractor was asked to forswear any side arrangements with the vendor as a condition of the contract.
examples.analytical: The court held that the witness had forsworn himself by knowingly giving false testimony after swearing to tell the truth.

nuance.analogy: It is like signing a formal oath in ink: once it is sworn, it is hard to take back, and breaking it means you have forsworn yourself.
nuance.etymology: From Old English forswerian, meaning to swear falsely or to renounce by oath, from for- (away, against) and swerian (to swear).
common_mistakes: Confusing forswear with forsake: forswear is about oaths and renunciation, while forsake is about abandoning people or things.
Using it in casual speech where give up or swear off would sound more natural.
nuance.biblical_note: The Greek and Hebrew texts discuss oaths and vows as serious commitments that God takes seriously. Matthew 5:33-37 teaches that disciples should not swear falsely but should let their yes be yes and their no be no. Numbers 30:2 says a person who makes a vow to the LORD must not break his word, which shows the cost of breaking an oath.

forswear.etymology: From Middle English *forsweren*, from Old English *forswerian* (“to swear falsely”).

senses.definition: The ordinal form of the number forty-nine, describing a person or thing in position number 49 of a sequence.
senses.example: The answer appears on the forty-ninth page of the book.

senses.definition: One of forty-nine equal parts of a whole.
senses.example: A forty-ninth of 980 is 20.

core.definition: Coming in position number 49 in a series; the ordinal form of forty-nine.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the word ninth, with the main vowel in NINE. The -th at the end is voiceless, and the nth cluster is pronounced with a clear n before the th.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it is just a number word.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use forty-ninth for positions like rows, floors, or editions. In speech, people often say the forty-ninth row or the forty-ninth floor. In writing, numerals like 49th are common.

distinctions.note: Forty-nine is the cardinal number for a quantity; forty-ninth is the ordinal for a position.
Fiftieth is the next position after forty-ninth; use it when counting toward the end of a series.

examples.everyday: Our apartment is on the forty-ninth floor, so the elevator takes a while.
