core.definition: In a way that does not use violence; peacefully, especially in protest or resistance.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on VY. The 'vi' is 'vy', and the final 'ly' is a clear 'lee'.

nuance.connotation: Positive or neutral. It highlights restraint, often in political or social contexts.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use nonviolently to describe how people protested, resisted or settled disputes, such as 'They protested nonviolently.' In casual talk, people might say 'peacefully' instead. It is most common in news reports, political speech and history.

distinctions.note: Peacefully describes a calm manner in general; nonviolently emphasizes the deliberate choice to avoid violence, especially under provocation.
Calmly describes an emotional state; nonviolently describes a method of acting or resisting.

examples.everyday: The neighbors settled their fence dispute nonviolently, by talking it over with the county surveyor.
examples.professional: We agreed to handle the vendor conflict nonviolently, through formal mediation rather than escalation.
examples.analytical: Movements that act nonviolently often sustain moral legitimacy even when facing brutal repression.

nuance.analogy: Like a referee who calls a foul without raising a fist, the outcome is decided by rules rather than force.
nuance.etymology: From nonviolent plus the adverb suffix -ly.
common_mistakes: Writing 'nonviolently' with the stress on the wrong syllable; the stress is on VY.
Using nonviolently as a synonym for 'quietly', which changes the meaning from avoiding force to avoiding noise.

senses.definition: A symbol or annotation.
senses.example: The chemist wrote a small note beside each formula to explain the notation in her lab notebook.

senses.definition: A mark or token by which a thing may be known; a visible sign; a character; a distinctive mark or feature; a characteristic quality.
senses.example: Humility was a recurring note in the sermons that made him so admired by the congregation.

senses.definition: A mark, or sign, made to call attention, to point out something to notice, or the like; a sign, or token, proving or giving evidence.
senses.example: The spike in missing values was a clear note that the sensor had failed.

senses.definition: A brief remark; a marginal comment or explanation; hence, an annotation on a text or author; a comment; a critical, explanatory, or illustrative observation.
senses.example: She wrote a short note in the margin explaining the author's odd citation.

senses.definition: A written or printed communication or commitment.
senses.example: I left him a note to remind him to take out the trash.

senses.definition: A brief piece of writing intended to assist the memory; a memorandum; a minute.
senses.example: I left him a note to remind him to take out the trash.

senses.definition: A short informal letter; a billet.
An academic treatise (often without regard to length); a treatment; a discussion paper; (loosely) any contribution to an academic discourse.
senses.example: Her short note on Bayesian priors was published in the journal's methods section.

senses.definition: A diplomatic missive or written communication.
A written or printed paper (or digital equivalent) acknowledging a debt, and promising payment.
senses.example: a promissory note

senses.definition: A piece of paper or polymer money; a banknote.
senses.example: I didn't have any coins to pay with, so I used a note.

senses.definition: A small size of paper used for writing letters or notes.
senses.example: I ordered the small note size stationery for thank-you letters to donors.

senses.definition: A character, variously formed, to indicate the length of a tone, and variously placed upon the staff to indicate its pitch.
senses.example: The quarter note gets one beat, while the half note lasts twice as long.

senses.definition: A musical sound; a tone; an utterance; a tune; a beat of a drum.
senses.example: She hit a clear, high note that echoed through the cathedral.

senses.definition: A key of the piano or organ.
senses.example: The middle C note on our old upright piano sticks every time.

senses.definition: A call or song of a bird.
senses.example: At dawn, the robin's sweet note carried across the frozen lake.

senses.definition: An indicator to which the player must correctly time some input.
senses.example: In the rhythm game, I missed the note and lost my combo.

senses.definition: An element of a scent, fragrance, or perfume, especially as a descriptor or category.
senses.example: The perfume's top note is bright citrus, fading into sandalwood.

senses.definition: Observation; notice; heed.
senses.example: The manager took note of the complaints and changed the schedule.

senses.definition: Reputation; distinction.
senses.example: a poet of note

senses.definition: A critical comment.
senses.example: Your performance was fantastic! I have just one note: you were a little flat in bars 35 and 36.

senses.definition: That which is needed or necessary; business; duty; work.
senses.example: Her note at the mill was the bookkeeping, which she did before dawn.

senses.definition: Milk-giving by a cow or sow; the period following calving or farrowing, during which a cow or sow is most productive and useful.
senses.example: The heifer came into her first note after calving in early spring.

senses.definition: (The addition of quotations indicative of this usage is being sought:) The milk given by a cow or sow during such period.
senses.example: The farmer weighed each cow's note at the morning milking.

senses.definition: A sound.
To notice with care; to observe; to remark; to heed.
senses.example: If you look to the left, you can note the old cathedral.

senses.definition: To record in writing; to make a memorandum of.
senses.example: We noted his speech.

senses.definition: To denote; to designate.
senses.example: The modular multiplicative inverse of x may be noted x.

senses.definition: To annotate.
To set down in musical characters.
To record on the back of (a bill, draft, etc.) a refusal of acceptance, as the ground of a protest, which is done officially by a notary.

core.definition: A short written message or record, or a brief piece of paper with information, used to remind or communicate.

pronunciation.tip: The vowel is a diphthong that glides from 'oh' toward 'oo,' so do not stop at a pure 'o' sound. The final t is released clearly in careful speech and often flapped or softened in fast speech.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and friendly. A handwritten note often feels personal and warm, while a formal note in business is more neutral.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use note for quick written messages, reminders, and thank-you cards, and also for a brief official communication. In school, people say 'take notes,' not 'do notes.' For paper money, Americans usually say 'bill' rather than 'note,' so 'a five-dollar bill' is the natural phrase.

distinctions.note: A memo is usually a formal internal business communication, while a note is typically shorter and more personal.
A notice is a public or official announcement, while a note is a message written for one person or a small group.
An annotation is a comment added to a text or image, while a note can be any short written record.

examples.everyday: Could you leave a note for Jake saying I'll be a little late for dinner?
examples.professional: I've added a note to the ticket explaining why we changed the threshold for the alert.
examples.analytical: The author's note at the end of the chapter explains how the data were cleaned and why outliers were removed.

nuance.analogy: A note is a signpost you leave for your future self or for someone else on the same road.
nuance.etymology: From Latin nota, 'a mark, sign.'
common_mistakes: Saying 'do notes' in class; Americans say 'take notes.'
Using 'note' for paper money; Americans usually say 'bill.'

note.etymology: From Middle English *note*, from Old English *not*, *nōt* (“note, mark, sign”) and Old French *note* (“letter, note”), both from Latin *nota* (“mark, sign, remark, note”).

senses.definition: The act of nourishing or the state of being nourished.
senses.example: Fresh vegetables and whole grains provide the nourishment a growing child needs.

senses.definition: Something that nourishes; food.

core.definition: Food or other substances that feed the body and help it grow and stay healthy; also the act of nourishing.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, and keep the r rhotic. The middle syllable 'ish' is short and light, and the final 'ment' is unstressed, so it sounds like 'ment,' not 'ment' with a full 'eh' vowel.

nuance.connotation: Positive. It suggests something beneficial and necessary, and it is often used figuratively for emotional or spiritual support.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use nourishment in health, nutrition, and cooking contexts, such as 'a source of nourishment,' and in figurative speech about emotional or spiritual needs. In everyday talk, people usually say 'food' or 'something to eat'; nourishment sounds more careful or formal. It often appears on nutrition labels and in health writing.

distinctions.note: Food is the everyday, general word for things we eat; nourishment emphasizes the benefit food gives to the body.
Nutrition is the science or process of getting nutrients from food; nourishment is the result of that process.

examples.everyday: After the long hike, we stopped at a diner and got some real nourishment, like eggs and toast.
examples.professional: The cafeteria redesign aims to provide balanced nourishment for staff working long shifts.
examples.analytical: Many philosophers argue that wisdom is a form of spiritual nourishment, not merely a store of information.

nuance.analogy: Nourishment is like fuel for a car: it is the thing that actually gets the engine running.
nuance.etymology: From nourish plus the suffix -ment, from Old French norrir, 'to feed.'
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the middle syllable as a full vowel, as in 'nour-ish-MENT'; the stress belongs on the first syllable.
Using nourishment as a countable noun in the plural for general food; say 'food' or 'nutrients' for everyday counting.

nourishment.etymology: From Middle English *norisshement*, from Middle French, from Old French *norissement*, from *norrir*, equivalent to *nourish* + *-ment*.

senses.definition: A gentle push.
senses.example: give someone a nudge

senses.definition: A feature of instant messaging software used to get the attention of another user, as by shaking the conversation window or playing a sound.
senses.example: She sent me a nudge in the chat window because I hadn't replied in an hour.

senses.definition: The rotation by one step of a fruit machine reel of the player's choice.
senses.example: Since the machine was showing two lemons and a cherry, I decided to try a nudge.

senses.definition: The use of positive reinforcement and indirect suggestions as ways to influence.
senses.example: Behavioral economists rely on nudges, such as default enrollment, to shape people's savings decisions.

senses.definition: To push against gently, especially in order to gain attention or give a signal.
senses.example: Could you nudge the monitor a little to the left so I can see the screen?

senses.definition: To near or come close to something.
senses.example: This year's profits are nudging the 10 million mark.

senses.definition: To move slightly.
senses.example: The line of cars nudged forward inch by inch as the light turned green.

core.definition: A gentle push, especially to get someone's attention or to encourage them to act.

pronunciation.tip: The vowel is the short uh of hug and bus, not the oo of food. The final dge is pronounced like j in judge.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to mildly positive; it suggests a light, friendly encouragement rather than pressure.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use nudge constantly in everyday life, at work and in policy discussions. A friend might say give me a nudge if I forget something, and a natural reply is thanks for the nudge. Nudge theory, from behavioral economics, is a common term in American news and business writing.

distinctions.note: Push can be forceful or neutral; nudge is always gentle and small.
Prod suggests poking someone who is reluctant to act; nudge is softer and friendlier.
Shove is a forceful move and can be rude or aggressive; nudge is never violent.

collocations: nudge someone in the right direction

examples.everyday: Can you give me a nudge if I start talking too long at dinner?
examples.professional: I'll send a quick nudge to the team so they finish their reviews by Friday.
examples.analytical: Behavioral economists argue that a well-designed default can nudge people toward better savings choices without restricting their freedom.

nuance.analogy: Like a light tap on the shoulder that says look over here, a nudge guides without forcing.
common_mistakes: Using nudge for a hard or accidental push; it always implies a gentle touch.
Saying nudge to someone to do; the correct pattern is nudge someone to do something, with the object before to.

nudge.etymology: Circa 17th century, perhaps of origin, related to, *nyggje* (“to push, rub, shove”), from the root of Proto-Germanic **hnōjaną* (“to smooth, join together”), from Proto-Indo-European **kneh₂-*.

senses.definition: Quantity of countable things.
senses.example: Any number of people can be reading from a given repository at a time.

senses.definition: An abstract entity used to describe quantity.
senses.example: Zero, one, −1, 2.5, and pi are all numbers.

senses.definition: A numeral: a symbol for a non-negative integer.
senses.example: The number 8 is usually made with a single stroke.

senses.definition: An element of one of several sets: natural numbers, integers, rational numbers, real numbers, complex numbers, and sometimes extensions such as hypercomplex numbers, etc.
senses.example: The equation eiπ+1=0 includes the most important numbers: 1, 0, π, i, and e.

senses.definition: Indicating the position of something in a list or sequence. Abbreviations: No or No. no or no. (in each case, sometimes written with a superscript "o", like Nº or №). The symbol "#" is also used in this manner.
senses.example: Horse number 5 won the race.

senses.definition: A sequence of digits and letters used to register people, automobiles, and various other items.
senses.example: Her passport number is C01X864TN.

senses.definition: A telephone number.
senses.example: Let's give her a call. Do you have her number handy?

senses.definition: Of a word or phrase, the state of being singular, dual or plural, shown by inflection.
senses.example: Adjectives and nouns should agree in gender, number, and case.

senses.definition: Poetic meters; verses, rhymes.
senses.example: The poet's odes flowed in graceful numbers that charmed the old professor.

senses.definition: A performance; especially, a single song or song and dance routine within a larger show.
senses.example: For his second number, he sang "The Moon Shines Bright".

senses.definition: A group of people.
senses.example: I include myself in their number.

senses.definition: A person.
senses.example: Who's that number in the red coat talking to Dana?

senses.definition: An outfit, particularly a stylish one.
senses.example: She showed up in a sleek black number that turned every head.

senses.definition: A marijuana cigarette, or joint; also, a quantity of marijuana bought from a dealer.
senses.example: He rolled a number and passed it around the back porch.

senses.definition: A large amount, in contrast to a smaller amount; numerical preponderance.
senses.example: Large numbers of volunteers showed up despite the freezing rain.

senses.definition: An activity; assignment; job, as in cushy number.
senses.example: He landed a cushy number at the consulting firm, with no weekend work.

senses.definition: Something that numbs.
senses.example: The doctor gave him a strong number before the surgery.

senses.definition: (dated) An issue of a periodical publication.
senses.example: the latest number of a magazine
senses.label: dated

senses.definition: To total or count; to amount to.
senses.example: I don’t know how many books are in the library, but they must number in the thousands.

senses.definition: To limit to a certain number; to reckon (as by fate) to be few in number.
senses.example: The old man knew that his days were numbered.

senses.definition: To label (items) with numbers; to assign numbers to (items).
senses.example: Number the baskets so that we can find them easily.

senses.definition: To call out and assign a series of numbers (usually to people), either for the sake of dividing into groups or for counting.
senses.example: Shelley numbered off the group into two teams for the baseball game.

senses.definition: To enumerate or list, especially while assigning numbers to.
senses.example: Please number each page before you staple the report together.

senses.definition: To classify or include (in a group of things).
senses.example: Alexander the Great's army numbered an elite cavalry among its ranks.

senses.definition: To be classified or included (in a certain group or category of things).
senses.example: Her horses number among the fastest in her country.

core.definition: A numeral or string of digits used to count, measure or identify something, such as a phone number.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, NUM, and reduce the second syllable to a soft 'er' with no separate vowel. Pronounce the b clearly; it is not silent, and do not say 'NOOM-ber'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a practical, everyday word with no emotional charge.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use number constantly for phone numbers, account numbers and room numbers, and for quantities like 'a number of people'. In a phrase like 'a number of' the verb agrees with the plural noun, so 'a number of people are coming', while 'the number of' takes a singular verb. In speech people often say 'What's your number?' to ask for a phone number.

distinctions.note: A number is the value itself, while a numeral is the symbol that represents it, so 7 is a numeral that names the number seven.
Figure is often used in the plural for statistics or amounts of money, and it sounds more formal in business settings.

examples.everyday: What's your phone number, so I can text you when we get to the restaurant?
examples.professional: Can you send me the order number so I can track the shipment before the meeting?
examples.analytical: The number of parameters in a model must be weighed against the sample size, or the model will fit noise rather than signal.

nuance.analogy: A number is like a person's address: the same house can be described in words, but the number gives you an exact, unique way to find it.
nuance.etymology: From Latin numerus, meaning 'a number, a count, or a reckoning'.
common_mistakes: Using much with numbers, as in 'much numbers'; say 'many numbers' or 'large numbers'.
Using a singular verb after 'a number of' (say 'a number of people are coming', not 'is coming').

core.definition: In the Bible, the father of Joshua, from the tribe of Ephraim. Also the Hebrew letter nun, the fourteenth letter of the Hebrew alphabet.

pronunciation.tip: Pronounce it as one long, stressed syllable, like the English word 'noon'. Do not confuse it with 'nun' (a religious sister), which is a separate word, though it is spelled the same.

nuance.connotation: Neutral
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this word almost only in Bible study, theology, and discussions of Hebrew. In everyday English, 'nun' means a woman who belongs to a religious community, so context usually makes the meaning clear. In a Bible class, you would say 'Joshua the son of Nun' with the name stressed.

distinctions.note: Spelled and pronounced the same, but the biblical name is a male name for Joshua's father, while the common word refers to a woman in religious life.

examples.everyday: My Bible study leader said Joshua's father was named Nun, which surprised me.
examples.professional: In my seminar handout, I listed Nun as Joshua's father, with the references in Numbers and Joshua.
examples.analytical: The genealogical formula 'Joshua the son of Nun' links Joshua to the Ephraimite line and establishes his authority as Moses' successor.

nuance.analogy: Like a family name that tells you whose child someone is: 'Joshua, Nun's son'.
nuance.etymology: Hebrew nun, of uncertain meaning; possibly related to 'fish' or 'continuance', but this is not certain.
common_mistakes: Saying the biblical name with a short vowel, like 'nun' in 'sun'; it is a long vowel, like 'noon'.
Assuming it always means a religious woman; in Bible contexts it is a man's name.
nuance.biblical_note: Nun (Hebrew nun) is the father of Joshua, who led Israel into the Promised Land. The Bible identifies Joshua as 'the son of Nun' to show his tribal and family background. Exodus 33:11 calls Joshua Moses' young assistant, Numbers 13:8 lists Nun's son among the Israelite spies, and Joshua 1:1 names Joshua as the son of Nun when he takes over leadership after Moses' death.

nun.etymology: From Middle English *nonne*, *nunne*, from Old English *nunne* (“nun”), from Late Latin *nonna* (“nun, tutor”), originally (along with masculine form *nonnus* (“man”)) a term of address for elderly persons, perhaps, reminiscent of *nana*, like *papa* etc.

senses.definition: In the state of suckling young, lactating.
senses.example: The nursing bear wouldn't move far until her cubs were older.

senses.definition: Referring to nurses.
senses.example: The nursing staff worked overtime at the hospital.

senses.definition: Suckling, such as breastfeeding.
senses.example: The lactation consultant explained that nursing usually gets easier after the first two weeks.

senses.definition: The process or profession of caring for patients as a nurse.
senses.example: She went into nursing as a career.

core.definition: The profession of caring for sick, injured, or disabled people, usually under a doctor's direction.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable. The final -ing is a short 'ih' sound, as in 'sit,' not the long 'ee' sound of 'sing' in some accents.

nuance.connotation: Positive. It suggests skill, compassion, and public service, and it is respected in American culture.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say 'I'm in nursing school' or 'She works in nursing' for the profession. 'Nursing' is also a common everyday word for breastfeeding, as in 'She's nursing the baby,' and in 'nursing bra.' As an adjective, 'nursing mother' describes a mother who is breastfeeding. Nursing homes are called 'skilled nursing facilities' in formal contexts.

distinctions.note: 'Nurse' names the person, while 'nursing' names the profession or the act of caring for someone.
'Breastfeeding' is the clearer and more clinical term, while 'nursing' is common in everyday speech for the same act.

examples.everyday: My sister is finishing her nursing degree next spring, and she's already working part-time at the hospital.
examples.professional: The hospital is hiring more nursing staff for the night shift because patient volume has increased.
examples.analytical: Florence Nightingale helped turn nursing into a disciplined profession grounded in evidence and training.

nuance.analogy: Like a bridge between a patient's fear and the care of doctors, nursing is the steady work that holds everything together.
nuance.etymology: From the verb nurse plus -ing, from Middle English nursen, from Old French norrice 'nurse.'
common_mistakes: Saying 'I am a nursing' instead of 'I am a nurse' or 'I am in nursing.'
Assuming 'nursing' always means healthcare; in American conversation it often means breastfeeding.

senses.definition: Of or pertaining to oblation; oblational.

core.definition: Relating to an offering made to God, especially a sacrifice or oblation.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, AH. The middle syllables are reduced to 'bluh-tuh', and the final -ory is 'ree' with the vowel of 'cot', matching the cot-caught merger common in the US.

nuance.connotation: Neutral: it is a precise religious descriptor without judgment.
nuance.usage_note: Technical and theological, used in liturgical and academic writing. Americans rarely say it aloud; in everyday English they would say 'offering' or 'sacrificial'. You will meet it in discussions of the Eucharist, monastic life and biblical sacrifice.

distinctions.note: Sacrificial is common and general, stressing giving up something dear; oblatory stresses the formal act of offering something to God.
Votive refers to a gift or candle given to fulfill a vow; oblatory describes the act of offering in worship more broadly.

examples.professional: The grant proposal framed the community kitchen as an oblatory project, returning resources to the neighborhood that supported us.
examples.analytical: Hebrews reads Christ's death as an oblatory act, a single self-offering that completes the sacrificial system.

nuance.analogy: An oblatory act is like a gift set on an altar: it is given away on purpose, with its recipient in mind.
nuance.etymology: From oblation, from Latin oblatio, an offering, from offerre, to offer.
common_mistakes: Confusing it with 'obligatory', which means required
Using it casually for any kind of giving
Stressing the middle syllable
nuance.biblical_note: The Hebrew word qorban, meaning that which is brought near, names Old Testament offerings. Leviticus 1:2 describes bringing an offering to the LORD from livestock or flock. Hebrews 10:10 says believers are made holy through the offering of Christ's body once for all, using the Greek word prosphora. Romans 15:16 speaks of the offering of the Gentiles, made holy by the Holy Spirit.

traditions.view: The Divine Liturgy is understood as an offering of bread and wine that become the body and blood of Christ, offered to the Father in thanksgiving and memorial.
The Mass is a sacrifice that makes present Christ's one sacrifice on the cross, offered sacramentally in the Eucharist.

Most Protestant traditions reject the Mass as a repeated sacrifice and affirm Christ's once-for-all atonement. Lutheran and Reformed churches speak of the Supper in terms of thanksgiving and communion, while many Baptist and free churches treat it primarily as a memorial.

senses.definition: To notice or view, especially carefully or with attention to detail.
senses.example: From this vantage point we can observe the behavior of the animals in their natural habitat.

senses.definition: To follow or obey the custom, practice, or rules (especially of a religion).
senses.example: Please observe all posted speed limits.

senses.definition: To take note of and celebrate (a holiday or similar occurrence), to keep; to follow (a type of time or calendar reckoning).
senses.example: Our family observes Passover with a seder and a long dinner every spring.

senses.definition: To comment on something; to make an observation.
senses.example: The senator observed that the bill would be detrimental to his constituents.

senses.definition: An observation (remark, comment or judgment).
senses.example: The old professor's wry observe about grading made the whole class laugh.

core.definition: To watch or notice something carefully, especially in order to learn about it or record it.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the second syllable, ZURV, and the first syllable is a weak schwa. The final v is voiced, so do not devoice it to 'f', and do not stress the first syllable.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It describes careful watching, which can be positive in science and negative only in the sense of spying.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say observe in science, police reports and formal writing, while everyday talk prefers watch or notice. In religion, to observe a holiday or the Sabbath means to keep it. The noun sense 'a remark' is old-fashioned, so say comment or observation instead.

distinctions.note: Watch is general and everyday; observe implies careful attention and sometimes recording.
Notice means becoming aware of something; observe implies deliberate attention over time.
Obey means following orders or commands; observe, in the religious sense, means keeping a custom or rule that you choose to honor.

examples.everyday: I like to observe the birds from my kitchen window in the morning.
examples.professional: We observed a 20 percent drop in latency after the rollout, so we are keeping the change.
examples.analytical: Careful theologians observe that Scripture speaks in many literary genres, and each genre requires its own kind of reading.

nuance.analogy: Like a bird-watcher who sits still and waits, so that the bird behaves as it normally does.
nuance.etymology: From Latin observare, 'to watch over, keep, obey'.
common_mistakes: Stressing the first syllable as OB-zerv; the stress belongs on the second syllable.
Using observe with to in the sense of 'to comment'; say observe that, or make an observation.
nuance.biblical_note: In Galatians 4:10 Paul is concerned that the Galatian believers are observing special days, months, seasons and years, which is a practice of religious calendar keeping. The Greek verb there is paratēreō, meaning to watch closely or keep a close eye on. In Matthew 23:2-3 Jesus tells the crowd and his disciples to observe what the scribes and Pharisees teach, but not to imitate their deeds, using the Greek verb tēreō, meaning to keep or guard.

traditions.view: Observance centers on the liturgical cycle, including Sunday worship, feast days and fasting seasons. Many feasts are dated by the church calendar, and some Orthodox churches still follow the Julian reckoning for them.
The Church requires attendance at Sunday Mass and on holy days of obligation, and it prescribes fasting and abstinence during Lent and on certain days. These are binding precepts of the Church.

Practice varies: Reformed and many Presbyterian churches stress observance of the Lord's Day, Lutherans and Anglicans keep the church year with Christmas, Easter and Pentecost, and Baptists and Pentecostals focus on Sunday worship and the Lord's Supper. Seventh-day Adventists and other Sabbatarian groups observe Saturday as the Sabbath.

observe.etymology: From Middle French *observer*, from Old French *observer*, from Latin *observō* (“to watch”), from *ob-* (“before”) + *servō* (“to keep”), from Proto-Indo-European **ser-* (“to guard”).

senses.definition: No longer in use or no longer useful; now disused or neglected (often in favor of something newer, better, or more fashionable); outmoded.
senses.example: Speedy, worldwide, accessible delivery of news through the Web has made newspapers obsolete.

senses.definition: Imperfectly developed; not very distinct.
senses.example: The faint, obsolete markings on the ancient coin were hard to make out under the dim museum lights.

senses.definition: To cause to become obsolete.
senses.example: This software component has been obsoleted.

senses.definition: An obsolete thing or person.
senses.example: The museum keeps every obsolete from the early computer era in climate-controlled rooms downstairs.

core.definition: No longer useful or used, usually because something newer or better has replaced it.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, AHB. The middle is a reduced 'uh', and the final syllable is 'leet', not 'let'.

nuance.connotation: Negative or neutral, implying something has lost its usefulness; it can sound dismissive when said about people.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say 'obsolete' about technology, equipment, and methods, as in 'This software is obsolete.' In casual talk, people often say 'outdated' or 'old-school' instead. Saying someone's skills are obsolete can sound harsh, so use it with care.

distinctions.note: Outdated is the everyday choice, while obsolete is stronger and more final, implying something is no longer used at all.
Antiquated suggests old-fashioned charm or quaintness, while obsolete suggests practical uselessness.

examples.everyday: My old flip phone is basically obsolete now, so I finally switched to a smartphone.
examples.professional: Our reporting dashboard is obsolete, so we're migrating everything to the new analytics platform this quarter.
examples.analytical: Some philosophical concepts have become obsolete, not because they were refuted, but because the questions they addressed no longer seem urgent.

nuance.analogy: An obsolete tool is like a rotary phone in a smartphone world: it still works, but nobody reaches for it anymore.
nuance.etymology: From Latin obsoletus, worn out or disused, past participle of obsolescere, to fall into disuse.
common_mistakes: Stressing the second syllable, as in 'ob-SO-leet'.
Using 'obsolete' to mean 'obscure' or 'rare'; obsolete means no longer in use, not merely uncommon.

obsolete.etymology: Latin *obsolētus* (“worn out, gone out of use”), past participle of *obsolesco* (“to wear out, fall into disuse, grow old, decay”); see *obsolesce*.

senses.definition: In an octahedral manner.

core.definition: In an octahedral way, meaning arranged so that items point to the corners of an octahedron around a central point.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the HEE syllable, then reduce the middle to a quick 'druh' and end with 'lee.' Avoid pronouncing the final -ally with a full 'al' vowel.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it is a very specialized technical adverb used in chemistry and crystallography.
nuance.usage_note: Octahedrally is rare and almost always technical, appearing in chemistry and crystallography, as in 'octahedrally coordinated.' Americans usually say 'in an octahedral arrangement' instead of using the adverb. Outside science it would sound unnatural.

distinctions.note: Tetrahedrally describes arrangement around four points, while octahedrally describes arrangement around six points at the corners of an octahedron.

examples.everyday: The gem cutter said the stone is cut octahedrally, so it sparkles from eight directions.
examples.professional: The model places each oxygen atom octahedrally around the metal center.
examples.analytical: The ligands must be arranged octahedrally for the crystal field splitting to take the form the textbook describes.

nuance.analogy: Like placing six balls around a center so each one touches the corners of an octahedron.
nuance.etymology: From octahedral, from octahedron (Greek oktaedron, eight-faced), with the adverb suffix -ly.
common_mistakes: Using octahedrally before a noun; say 'octahedral' as an adjective, as in 'an octahedral crystal.'
Mispronouncing the middle syllables as 'OCK-tuh-HED-ruh-lee.'

senses.definition: The quality of being offensive.

core.definition: The quality of being offensive, meaning the power of something to hurt, insult or disgust people.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the second syllable, FEN, and end with a short, reduced 'nus' sound. Do not stress the final syllable.

nuance.connotation: Negative; it names a quality that people find upsetting or insulting.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use offensiveness mainly in discussions about speech, media, advertising and public standards. In everyday talk they usually say 'how offensive it is' or 'that's offensive'. It is useful in essays and debates when you want to name the quality rather than the thing itself.

distinctions.note: Offense is an insult or hurt that happens, while offensiveness is the quality that makes something capable of causing offense.
Rudeness is a lack of good manners in a moment, while offensiveness describes content or behavior measured by its effect on people.

examples.everyday: I don't see the offensiveness in that joke, but my sister clearly does.
examples.professional: The moderation team scores each post for offensiveness before deciding whether to remove it.
examples.analytical: The debate turns on whether offensiveness is a property of words or of the audience who hears them.

nuance.analogy: Like a smell in a room: the quality is in the air, but it is only noticed by the person who breathes it.
nuance.etymology: From offensive, from Late Latin offensivus, from offendere, 'to strike against', with the suffix -ness.
common_mistakes: Using offensiveness as a count noun with an article, as in 'an offensiveness'; it is usually uncountable.
Confusing offensiveness with offense; use offense for the insult itself.

senses.definition: Following the intended route.
Proceeding smoothly as planned.
senses.example: Despite the setbacks, the migration project is still on course for March.

senses.definition: Likely to happen or to undergo something.
senses.example: Given the rising interest rates, the market is on course for a correction.

core.definition: Following the intended route or plan, and making progress as expected toward a goal.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on 'course', which has a clear r sound. Do not stress 'on', and do not add an extra vowel between the r and s.

nuance.connotation: Positive, meaning progress is going well and the plan is working.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'on course' in business, sports, and everyday planning: 'We are on course to finish early'. It often pairs with 'for' or 'to', as in 'on course for a record year'. 'Off course' is the usual opposite, and 'on track' is a close and very common synonym.

distinctions.note: 'On track' emphasizes progress toward a schedule or goal, while 'on course' emphasizes following the planned route.
'On schedule' refers specifically to time, while 'on course' covers direction and overall progress.

examples.everyday: We are on course to get to the airport early, so there is no reason to rush.
examples.professional: The project is on course for the June release, pending the final security review.
examples.analytical: Her argument stays on course only if we accept its initial premise about moral agency.

nuance.analogy: Being on course is like a ship that keeps its heading despite the wind, adjusting slightly to stay on the planned line.
nuance.etymology: 'Course' comes from Latin 'cursus', meaning 'a running' or 'path', from 'currere', 'to run'.
common_mistakes: Saying 'on the course' when you mean the plan or progress; 'on the course' refers to a golf course or a race course.
Confusing 'on course' with 'of course', which is an expression of agreement.

senses.definition: A situation with no obstacles or limitations; a clear opportunity to act freely or without significant competition.
senses.example: Once the rival firm stumbled, we had an open field to grow our customer base without competition.

senses.definition: A large, unobstructed area of land with minimal cover, exposing troops to potential enemy fire with little opportunity to hide or take cover.
senses.example: The soldiers crossed the open field under heavy fire, with nothing but grass to hide behind.

core.definition: A large, flat area of land with few or no trees, buildings, or other obstacles; figuratively, a situation with no barriers to action.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on 'field', which is a long vowel like 'feel-d'. The first syllable 'open' gets a secondary stress and a reduced second syllable.

nuance.connotation: Neutral in the literal sense; positive in the figurative sense of having freedom to act.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use open field for land in rural settings, and in sports for an area where a runner or player has space away from defenders, as in breaking free in the open field. Figuratively, people say they have an open field when they have little competition. In casual talk, you might say The field is wide open to describe a competition with no clear favorite.

distinctions.note: A meadow is a grassy field, often with wildflowers, while an open field may be bare, rough, or used for crops.
A clearing is a small open space in a forest, while an open field is usually larger and not surrounded by trees.

collocations: break free in the open field

examples.everyday: We walked out into the open field behind the farm and let the dog run around.
examples.professional: The startup has an open field in this market since no competitor has launched a product for small businesses yet.
examples.analytical: Describing a situation as an open field implies that prior constraints have been removed, but it also hides the risk that nobody has yet built the necessary foundations.

nuance.analogy: Like an empty parking lot at midnight: nothing blocks your path, so you can go wherever you want.
nuance.etymology: Open comes from Old English opan; field comes from Old English feld.
common_mistakes: Saying in open field instead of in the open field when describing a sports play.
Pronouncing field with a short vowel, as in fill-d.

core.definition: A hill or ridge in ancient Jerusalem, south of the Temple Mount, where the city's walls and dwellings were extended.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, and the second syllable is a reduced vowel, so it sounds like 'OH-fuhl,' not 'oh-FEL.'

nuance.connotation: Neutral
nuance.usage_note: Ophel is used almost only in biblical, historical, and archaeological contexts. Americans who discuss Jerusalem's ancient geography, such as Bible teachers or archaeologists, use the name, while others would not recognize it. In a general conversation, 'the City of David' is more familiar.

distinctions.note: Zion was the name for the citadel or the wider hill of Jerusalem, while Ophel is a specific lower spur south of the Temple Mount.
City of David is a title for the oldest part of Jerusalem, and Ophel is a part of that area, so the two overlap but are not identical.

examples.everyday: We walked up the slope near Ophel while we were in Jerusalem, and our guide pointed out the old walls.
examples.professional: Our archaeology report describes the excavations at Ophel, which date to the period of the monarchy.
examples.analytical: Ophel is the ridge south of the Temple Mount, and 2 Chronicles 27:3 says Jotham built extensively on its wall.

nuance.analogy: Ophel is like the bulge of a hill that a city grew out from, a foothold between the older core and the newer neighborhoods.
nuance.etymology: From Hebrew ʿōphel, meaning 'swelling' or 'mound'.
common_mistakes: Stressing the second syllable, as in 'oh-FEL.'
Confusing Ophel with Zion, which is a broader term for Jerusalem's hill.
nuance.biblical_note: Ophel is a fortified spur of land in Jerusalem, lying between the City of David and the Temple Mount. Key passages: 2 Chronicles 27:3 says King Jotham built extensively on the wall of Ophel. Nehemiah 3:26 names the Nethinim who lived on Ophel and repaired the wall at the Water Gate. Nehemiah 11:21 says the Nethinim lived on Ophel in the time after the exile.

senses.definition: Someone who oppresses another or others.
senses.example: The villagers rose up against the tyrant, the oppressor who had seized their harvest.

core.definition: A person or group that treats others cruelly and unjustly, using power over them.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the middle syllable, PRES. The final -or is a weak, rhotic 'er' sound, not 'or' as in 'door'.

nuance.connotation: Strongly negative. Calling someone an oppressor is a serious accusation and implies moral wrongdoing.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use oppressor in political, social and religious discussions, often in sermons or about history. In everyday talk, calling a boss or a neighbor an oppressor can sound harsh or overly dramatic. Use it only when injustice is real.

distinctions.note: A tyrant is a ruler who holds absolute power, often a single person. An oppressor can be a person, a group or a system that treats others unjustly.
A persecutor targets people for their beliefs or identity, often through punishment. An oppressor more broadly denies people freedom or dignity.

collocations: defend the oppressed against the oppressor

examples.everyday: My grandmother called the old landlord an oppressor, because he raised the rent every single year.
examples.professional: We should not frame the other team as oppressors; they are just overloaded and under pressure.
examples.analytical: The prophets often describe God as the defender of the poor against the oppressor, linking justice with divine character.

nuance.analogy: An oppressor is like a heavy hand pressing down on someone who cannot push back.
nuance.etymology: From oppress, from Latin opprimere, to press down.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the final -or as 'or' rather than a reduced 'er'.
Using oppressor for a mere critic or strict boss, which exaggerates the situation.
nuance.biblical_note: In Hebrew the verb behind oppression is ʿāšaq (to oppress, to defraud), and related words describe the oppressor as one who crushes the weak. Psalm 72:4 (RSV) speaks of a just king who will defend the needy and crush the oppressor. Exodus 3:9 (RSV) says God has seen the oppression of his people by the Egyptians, showing that God attends to the suffering of the oppressed. Proverbs 14:31 (RSV) teaches that whoever oppresses a poor man reproaches his Maker, linking mistreatment of the poor with an offense against God.

oppressor.etymology: From Middle English *oppressour*, from Old French *opressor* and Latin *oppressor*; equivalent to *oppress* + *or*.

senses.definition: To choose not to participate in something.

core.definition: To choose not to take part in something that others are doing, such as a program, plan or activity.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on out, the particle, so say AHPT OWT with the strong beat on OWT. In fast speech, the t of opt links into the vowel of out, sounding like 'AHP-tout'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It describes a choice, sometimes with a slight sense of stepping away from something expected.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use opt out constantly in everyday life and at work, for things like email subscriptions, data sharing, school programs or insurance plans. Natural replies include I'll pass or No thanks, I'll opt out. It is fine in most settings, from casual talk to meetings.

distinctions.note: Opt in means to choose to take part; opt out means to choose not to take part.
Drop out means to quit something you started, such as school; opt out often refers to a choice made before participating or in a specific program.

examples.everyday: I opted out of the group chat, since the messages never stop coming at night.
examples.professional: Employees can opt out of the survey, but we encourage everyone to participate so the results are accurate.
examples.analytical: Dworkin argues that citizens cannot simply opt out of a political community whose laws shape their lives.

nuance.analogy: Opting out is like leaving a party early: you choose to step away from what everyone else is doing.
nuance.etymology: Opt comes from Latin optare, to choose; out is an English adverb meaning away from or outside.
common_mistakes: Dropping of after opt out when a noun follows, as in opt out the survey; use opt out of.
Stressing opt rather than out in a phrasal verb sentence.

conversation.text: You can opt out of the company's dental plan.
I opted out of those marketing emails.

senses.definition: Not compulsory; left to personal choice; elective.
senses.example: On that beach clothing is entirely optional.

senses.definition: Something that is not compulsory, especially part of an academic course.
senses.example: Most of my classmates skipped the optionals and focused only on the required courses.

senses.definition: In various programming languages, a kind of variable that is assigned a specific data type but may or may not hold an actual value.
senses.example: The function accepts an optional that defaults to null when no value is supplied.

core.definition: Not required; left to a person's choice.

pronunciation.tip: The word has three syllables, not four: the 'ti' in 'option' is pronounced 'sh,' so the word sounds like 'AHP-shun-ul.' Stress the first syllable only.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive. It signals freedom of choice, and it sounds reassuring when something is extra.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'optional' often in school, work, and shopping, as in 'the training is optional' or 'an optional add-on.' It is polite and neutral. In software, it also appears in technical terms like 'optional parameter,' so context matters.

distinctions.note: 'Voluntary' stresses a person's free decision to act; 'optional' describes a thing that is not required.
'Elective' is mainly used for school courses a student chooses; 'optional' is broader.

examples.everyday: Breakfast is optional at the hotel, but it's included in the price.
examples.professional: The workshop is optional, so attendance won't be tracked in the performance review.
examples.analytical: The sacrament, on this account, is not optional for the believer, though its external form may vary.

nuance.analogy: Like a side dish on a restaurant menu: you can order it, but the meal is complete without it.
nuance.etymology: From 'option' with the adjective suffix -al, from Latin optio, 'choice.'
common_mistakes: Pronouncing 'optional' with a hard 't' as 'OP-tion-al' with four syllables; the 'ti' is a 'sh' sound.
Using 'optional' as a noun in everyday speech; 'option' is the usual noun.

senses.definition: In an opulent manner.

core.definition: In a lavish, luxurious way, showing great richness, abundance and expense.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable and reduce the 'pu' to a quick 'yuh'. The '-ent' becomes 'unt', and the ending is a light 'lee'.

nuance.connotation: Positive for describing beauty and richness, but it can suggest excess or waste when used critically.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'opulently' mainly in descriptions of decor, hotels, dress or lifestyles, often in writing and journalism. In casual speech they say 'lavishly,' 'luxuriously' or 'fancy.' It sounds stiff if used for ordinary objects, so reserve it for truly grand settings.

distinctions.note: Lavishly stresses generous spending and abundance, while opulently emphasizes a rich, luxurious appearance.
Luxuriously focuses on comfort and pleasure, while opulently focuses on visual grandeur and display.

examples.everyday: The hotel lobby was opulently decorated, with gold leaf and chandeliers everywhere.
examples.professional: The brand's flagship store is opulently fitted out, which supports its premium price position.
examples.analytical: Medieval courts displayed power by living opulently, using wealth as a visible sign of favor and status.

nuance.analogy: Like a dessert with three kinds of cream, gold sprinkles and truffle on top: richness piled on richness.
nuance.etymology: From Latin opulentus, 'wealthy,' from ops, 'wealth.'
common_mistakes: Mispronouncing the first syllable as 'oh-PU-lent'.
Using 'opulently' to describe a person's manners; say 'opulent' or 'lavish' for a lifestyle.
Using it for ordinary, everyday objects, which sounds exaggerated.

senses.definition: Relating to an orchestra or to music played by an orchestra.
senses.example: orchestral music/piece/sound

senses.definition: (uncommon) An orchestral performance.
senses.example: We heard a fine orchestral last night at Symphony Hall, the Brahms especially.
senses.label: uncommon

core.definition: Relating to an orchestra, or to music written or performed for orchestra.

pronunciation.tip: Stress shifts to the middle syllable, KES, unlike 'orchestra', which is stressed on OR. The first syllable keeps a weaker secondary stress, and the ending is a reduced 'truhl'.

nuance.connotation: Positive or neutral. It describes sound or music, and it is often used as praise for a rich, full sound.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use orchestral mostly to describe music: an orchestral score, an orchestral arrangement or an orchestral piece. In casual talk you might say 'classical' or 'with a full orchestra' instead. Describing a pop song's sound as orchestral is a compliment. The noun use, as in an orchestral performance, is uncommon.

distinctions.note: Symphonic refers specifically to a symphony, a large multi-movement work; orchestral is broader and covers any music written for orchestra.
Instrumental means played on instruments, with or without voices; orchestral specifically refers to a full orchestra, a particular kind of instrumental group.

examples.everyday: I'm not really into classical music, but the orchestral parts in that movie were gorgeous.
examples.professional: We licensed an orchestral track for the video, since recording a full orchestra was too expensive.
examples.analytical: The orchestral texture of Mahler's late symphonies creates a dense interplay of voices that resists any single reading.

nuance.analogy: Orchestral is to music what full color is to a painting: many voices working together at once.
nuance.etymology: From orchestra, from Greek orchēstra; see orchestra.
common_mistakes: Stressing the first syllable, as in 'OR-kes-trul'; the stress falls in the middle, or-KES-trul.
Using orchestral for any big sound; it means relating to or written for an orchestra, so a big band sound is not orchestral.

senses.definition: The method in which love for others is prioritized, with those most closely related and in close proximity getting priority.
senses.example: The pastor preached on ordo amoris, teaching that we should first love family, then neighbors, then strangers.

core.definition: In Augustinian Christian thought, the proper order of love, in which we love God first and then other people according to their closeness and need.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on OR in the first word and MOR in the second, and the r sounds are clear. The -is ending is short, and the middle vowel is reduced.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and technical. It is a term used in theology and philosophy, not in ordinary talk.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this phrase in seminary, philosophy, and theology courses, especially when discussing Augustine. It is not used in everyday talk, though a pastor might use it when preaching about how to prioritize family and neighbors. The phrase is Latin, so most Americans would say the order of love.

distinctions.note: Ordo amoris concerns the proper arrangement of loves, while ordo salutis concerns the steps by which God saves a person.
Charity is the general theological virtue of love, while ordo amoris is a specific principle about how that love should be ordered among different objects.

examples.everyday: My pastor says we should keep our love in the right order, with God first and then our family and neighbors.
examples.professional: In the leadership training, we discussed the ordo amoris as a framework for balancing commitments to the team, family, and the wider community.
examples.analytical: Augustine's ordo amoris holds that love must be directed according to the true value of its objects, so that disordered love becomes the root of sin.

nuance.analogy: The ordo amoris is like a well-organized calendar, where the most important commitments get the first and most reliable slots.
nuance.etymology: From Latin ordo, order, and amor, love; the phrase is associated with Augustine of Hippo.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing ordo as or-doh with a long o in the second syllable, when the stress is on the first syllable.
Thinking it means a rule about who you may love rather than a principle of priority.

senses.definition: In an organizational manner.
With regard to organization or an organization.

core.definition: In a way that relates to how an organization is structured, managed, or run.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on the -ZAY- syllable, and the -ion ending is pronounced SHUN, not 'see-on.' The final -ally is usually reduced to -uh-lee, so do not give every syllable equal weight.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a precise, professional word that describes structure or management without praising or criticizing.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this word mostly in business, government, and academic writing, for example when discussing whether a team works well organizationally. In casual talk people say 'in how the company is set up' instead. It is rarely used in everyday conversation.

distinctions.note: Structurally refers to the physical or formal frame of something, while organizationally refers to how people, roles, and processes within an organization are arranged.

examples.everyday: My neighbor's HOA is a mess organizationally, so nothing ever gets done.
examples.professional: Organizationally, the new team reports directly to the VP, which should cut down on approval delays.
examples.analytical: The merger was successful financially but remained unstable organizationally, since the two cultures never fully integrated.

nuance.analogy: Organizationally is like the blueprint of a building: it shows the rooms and hallways, not the furniture or the people living inside.
nuance.etymology: From organize, from Medieval Latin organizare, from organum, 'instrument, tool.'
common_mistakes: Stressing the wrong syllable, as in 'or-guh-NIZ-ay-shun-lee.'
Confusing it with organizational, which is an adjective and cannot replace it in sentences that need an adverb.

senses.definition: Of, concerned with, or preoccupied with a world different from the tangible world, especially a fantasy, imaginary, or mystical world.
senses.example: Her otherworldly devotion led her to spend nights in silent prayer and fasting.

senses.definition: Odd and unfamiliar; strange, uncanny, weird.
senses.example: The empty hallway had an otherworldly quality that made her hair stand up.

senses.definition: Of, concerned with, or preoccupied with spiritual matters.
senses.example: Her otherworldly devotion led her to spend nights in silent prayer and fasting.

core.definition: Seeming to belong to a different, spiritual or imaginary world, not the ordinary physical one.

pronunciation.tip: The primary stress falls on WURL, the second part of the compound. The middle syllable -ther- is reduced, and the d in -ld- is often silent in casual speech, so it sounds like 'WUR-lee'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive. It can suggest beauty, mystery or wonder, and sometimes unease when it means strange or unnatural.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use otherworldly to describe art, music, landscapes, movies or beings that feel beautiful, mysterious or unlike ordinary life. It is common in reviews and casual conversation, for example 'That singer has an otherworldly voice.' For spiritual contexts, it can sound slightly poetic.

distinctions.note: Ethereal emphasizes lightness and delicacy. Otherworldly emphasizes a sense of being from a different realm or extremely unusual.
Supernatural refers to phenomena beyond natural laws, such as ghosts or magic. Otherworldly describes an impression of being from another world, without necessarily claiming a supernatural cause.

examples.everyday: The sunset over the lake looked so otherworldly that we just stood there and stared.
examples.professional: The demo's otherworldly graphics impressed the client, but the team still had to make the code run on normal laptops.
examples.analytical: Mystical writers often describe an otherworldly perspective that transcends everyday categories without rejecting the material world.

nuance.analogy: Like walking into a dream: the room is familiar in shape but everything about it feels from another place.
nuance.etymology: From other and world, plus the suffix -ly, meaning 'belonging to another world'.
common_mistakes: Splitting the word into 'other world ly' with stress on the wrong syllable.
Using otherworldly to mean 'otherwise' or 'different' in a neutral way; it usually implies strangeness or beauty.

senses.definition: Out of normal sequence.
senses.example: You've got my index cards out of order again.

senses.definition: Not functioning properly; not in working order.
senses.example: The lift is always out of order.

senses.definition: Inappropriate or unsuitable.
senses.example: I suppose my remarks about his wife were out of order.

senses.definition: Not in order: not according with e.g. the procedural rules governing formal meetings of a deliberative body.
senses.example: The chair ruled the motion out of order because it was not properly seconded under the bylaws.

senses.definition: Untidy.
senses.example: My desk is always out of order, but I know exactly where everything is.

core.definition: Not working properly, so it cannot be used; or inappropriate or unacceptable in a given situation.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on 'OR' in 'order'. The r is strongly pronounced, and the final 'er' is a reduced American schwa-r, so say 'OR-der' rather than 'OR-dur' with a British-style vowel.

nuance.connotation: Neutral when describing a machine. Negative when describing behavior.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'Out of order' on signs for broken elevators, restrooms, and ATMs. For a bus, a train, or an elevator, 'out of service' is also common. When used for behavior, it means 'inappropriate', as in 'That joke was out of order.' Asking 'Is this machine out of order?' is a natural question at a store or a gas station.

distinctions.note: 'Out of service' is preferred for transit and public utilities; 'out of order' is the common term for a broken machine or device.
'Out of line' describes rude or overstepping behavior; 'out of order' also covers broken machines and meanings of sequence.

collocations: the machine is out of order
that comment was out of order
the elevator is out of order

examples.everyday: Sorry, the ice machine is out of order, so you'll have to get drinks somewhere else.
examples.professional: The build server has been out of order since last night, so please hold off on merging until it's back up.
examples.analytical: A list that runs out of order cannot be read as a sequence of cause and effect, so the author's argument depends on preserving the original arrangement.

nuance.analogy: Like a clock with its hands jammed: it still exists on the wall, but it cannot tell you the time.
nuance.etymology: 'Out' and 'of' are Old English; 'order' comes from Latin 'ordo', meaning row or rank, through Old French.
common_mistakes: Saying 'out of order' with a British-style vowel in 'order', or dropping the r.
Confusing 'out of order' with 'out of service' for buses or trains; Americans favor 'out of service' for public transport.

senses.definition: Physically unfit.
Not in its usual or proper shape.
senses.example: The metal fender was out of shape after the minor collision.

core.definition: Physically unfit from lack of exercise; also, not in good or usual condition.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on SHAYP, and the long a is a clear diphthong. Do not reduce 'shape' to 'shup', and keep the 'of' weak as 'uv'.

nuance.connotation: Mildly negative when describing a person's fitness, though it is often said lightly or self-deprecatingly.
nuance.usage_note: Americans often say 'I'm out of shape' about themselves in a joking way, especially after a break from exercise or a long winter. Saying it about someone else can sound blunt, so use it gently. A natural reply is 'Me too, I need to start running again.'

distinctions.note: Unfit is more formal or clinical and sounds more serious, while out of shape is casual and usually describes temporary loss of fitness.
Out of condition is more formal and often used for athletes or equipment, while out of shape is the everyday American choice.

collocations: out of shape for a marathon

examples.everyday: I used to run every morning, but I've gotten pretty out of shape since the move.
examples.professional: Our release process has gotten out of shape since we added three new teams, so we need a clearer workflow.
examples.analytical: A church can grow out of shape with its own confession, becoming busy with activity while losing its center in Christ.

nuance.analogy: Like a tent left folded in a closet: it still works, but it needs to be unpacked and re-stretched before use.
nuance.etymology: 'Shape' comes from Old English gesceap, meaning creation or form.
common_mistakes: Saying 'I am out shape' without the preposition 'of'.
Confusing it with 'in shape', which means fit and healthy.

senses.definition: Unexpectedly; without warning or preparation.
senses.example: After I hadn’t heard from her in six months, she called me out of the blue to meet for lunch.

core.definition: Unexpectedly, without any warning or preparation.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on 'BLUE', and 'of the' is reduced to 'uv thuh'. Link the words quickly, so it sounds like 'owt-uv-thuh-BLOO', with the 'th' voiced in 'the'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral or slightly surprised. It describes an event that was unexpected, which can be good or bad depending on context.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this idiom in everyday conversation, such as 'The call came out of the blue'. It is casual and fits in both friendly talk and work conversation. A natural reply is 'Really? I had no idea', or 'That's a surprise'. It is not used for planned events.

distinctions.note: Suddenly describes speed, while out of the blue emphasizes that something was entirely unexpected and not signaled in advance.
Unexpectedly is neutral and general, while out of the blue is more informal and vivid.

examples.everyday: My old college roommate called me out of the blue last night, and we talked for an hour.
examples.professional: The client sent a termination notice out of the blue, so we need to plan a quick response.
examples.analytical: The phrase out of the blue captures the sense of an event that arrives without antecedent, which makes it useful for describing surprising shifts in argument.

nuance.analogy: Something out of the blue is like lightning on a clear day: there was no storm to warn you.
nuance.etymology: The phrase likely comes from the sense of a clear blue sky, where a sudden event seems to come from nowhere, and it appears in English from the 1800s.
common_mistakes: Saying 'from the blue', which is not the standard form.
Using the idiom for a planned visit, which would sound wrong.
Pronouncing 'blue' as 'blew', which is only the past tense of 'blow'.

out-of-the-blue.etymology: Short for out of the blue sky, likening an unexpected event to lightning or rain coming suddenly from a cloudless sky.

conversation.text: My old roommate called me out of the blue last week.
Out of the blue, the client asked for a new feature.
The storm came out of the blue and ruined our picnic.

senses.definition: The state of having complete legal control of something; possession; proprietorship.
Responsibility for or control over something.
senses.example: The successful candidate will take ownership of all internal design projects.

core.definition: The state of legally owning something; having the right to possess, use, and control it, or the responsibility for looking after it.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, OH. The middle syllable is a weak r-colored vowel, so say it as 'ner' with almost no vowel, not 'NAY-ner-ship'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a plain legal or practical term; it sounds positive when describing pride in a home or business, and serious when describing legal disputes.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use ownership for legal and everyday control of property, such as 'home ownership' or 'car ownership.' In conversation they often say 'Who owns this?' or 'It's mine,' and reserve 'ownership' for more formal talk about rights, contracts, or responsibility. It can also mean taking responsibility for a problem, as in 'take ownership of the project,' which is common in American workplaces.

distinctions.note: Possession is the physical holding or control of something; ownership is the legal right to it, so you can own a house you do not possess because you rent it out.
Property is the thing that is owned; ownership is the right or status of owning it.

examples.everyday: We're thinking about home ownership now that the rent keeps going up.
examples.professional: Before we merge the two accounts, we need to confirm ownership of the customer data.
examples.analytical: Locke grounds ownership in the labor a person mixes with what is found in nature, a claim that later theorists have questioned.

nuance.analogy: Ownership is like the deed in a drawer: it is the proof of who has the final say over the house, even when someone else is living in it.
nuance.etymology: Formed from own (from Old English agen, 'owned') with the suffix -ship, meaning 'state or condition of.'
common_mistakes: Saying 'the ownership of the car is mine' is fine, but avoid 'I have the ownership' in casual speech; 'I own it' is more natural.
Mispronouncing the middle syllable as a full vowel, such as 'OH-nur-SHIP' with a strong second syllable.

senses.definition: The process of reacting or treating something with oxygen.

core.definition: The process of treating or combining something with oxygen, such as adding oxygen to blood, water or a chemical reaction.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the syllable -NAY-, and the final -tion is pronounced 'shun' with a reduced vowel. The first syllable 'ox' sounds like 'ahks' in General American, with the cot vowel.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. The word is a neutral technical term with no emotional charge, though it is most often heard in medical or scientific settings.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this word mainly in medicine, biology, environmental science and engineering, for example when talking about blood oxygenation or water oxygenation in a lake. In everyday conversation people say 'getting enough oxygen' or 'oxygen levels' instead. The verb is 'oxygenate', and the opposite process is 'deoxygenation'.

distinctions.note: Oxidation is the broader chemical process of losing electrons, which often involves oxygen but not always, while oxygenation specifically means adding oxygen to something.
Aeration means mixing air into a liquid or soil, while oxygenation focuses on the oxygen content itself, so the two often overlap in pond or water management.

examples.everyday: The nurse said my husband's oxygenation was fine after the breathing treatment.
examples.professional: The lab report showed that the oxygenation of the sample dropped during the overnight run.
examples.analytical: The study measured tissue oxygenation to test whether the drug improved circulation or simply changed the readings.

nuance.analogy: Oxygenation is like filling a balloon with air: the gas goes into the liquid or tissue until it is fully carried there.
nuance.etymology: From oxygen plus the suffix -ation; oxygen comes from Greek oxys (sharp, acid) and -gen (producing).
common_mistakes: Misspelling it as 'oxigenation' with one x, which is an easy error because the word has no second x
Confusing it with oxidation, which is a different, broader chemical process
Using it in casual talk where 'oxygen levels' would sound more natural

senses.definition: In statistical significance testing, the probability of obtaining a test statistic at least as extreme as the one that was actually observed, assuming that the null hypothesis is true.

core.definition: The probability of getting a result at least as extreme as the one observed, assuming the null hypothesis is true.

pronunciation.tip: Say 'p' as the letter name 'pee', then stress 'VAL'. In fast speech the 'ue' of 'value' reduces to 'yoo', so it sounds like 'VAL-yoo'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and technical. It is a standard term in statistics and research reports.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'p-value' in statistics, science, business analytics, and research reporting. People often say 'the p-value is under point oh five' in meetings. Be careful: the p-value is not the probability that the hypothesis is true, and in casual talk it is often misunderstood.

distinctions.note: The significance level is a threshold chosen before the study, such as 0.05, while the p-value is calculated from the observed data.
A confidence interval gives a range of plausible effect sizes, while a p-value gives the probability of the data under the null hypothesis.

examples.everyday: The article said the result was significant with a p-value under 0.05, but I still don't know what that means.
examples.professional: The test came back with a p-value of 0.03, so we can say the difference is statistically significant.
examples.analytical: A p-value measures the compatibility of data with the null hypothesis, not the probability that the null is true.

nuance.analogy: A p-value is like a surprise meter: it tells you how unlikely the observed result would be if nothing interesting were happening.
nuance.etymology: From 'p' for probability and value, a modern term used in statistical testing.
common_mistakes: Saying the p-value is the probability that the hypothesis is true.
Pronouncing 'p' as a word instead of the letter name 'pee'.

senses.definition: Capable of being packed.
senses.example: The rain jacket is lightweight and packable, so it fits in my backpack.

senses.definition: Anything that can be packed for transportation.
senses.example: The outdoor store sells sleeping bags and other packables for backpacking trips.

core.definition: Designed to be folded or compressed so it fits easily into a bag or suitcase.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, PAK. The second syllable is a weak uh, and the -able ending is a reduced syllable pronounced bul, not bell or bl.

nuance.connotation: Positive. It describes a practical feature that makes an item convenient to carry.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use packable in shopping, travel, and outdoor contexts, especially for jackets, raincoats, and backpacks. Clothing companies often market packable jackets to travelers. It is informal and practical rather than formal, and people often use it as a selling point.

distinctions.note: Foldable emphasizes that something can be folded, while packable emphasizes that it fits well into a bag or pack.
Portable means easy to carry or move from place to place, often as a whole. Packable focuses on size when compressed.

examples.everyday: This jacket is packable, so I can stuff it into my backpack for the hike.
examples.professional: We need a packable version of the training kit so field staff can carry it on flights without paying oversize fees.
examples.analytical: The packable design trades bulk for durability, a tradeoff the review board weighed carefully before approving it.

nuance.analogy: A packable item is like a pocket map that folds small enough to fit anywhere but unfolds to show everything you need.
nuance.etymology: Formed from pack and the suffix -able, meaning able to be packed.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the final syllable as a full -abel with a long a sound.
Saying packable when you mean bulky or heavy; the word praises small, compressible size.

senses.definition: One who takes pains; a careful worker.
senses.example: Martha was a painstaker who checked every citation twice before the manuscript went to press.

core.definition: A person who works very carefully and thoroughly, paying close attention to every detail.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress is on PAYN and a weaker secondary stress falls on STAY. End with a reduced, r-colored 'ur' sound, not a full 'er' or 'ay.'

nuance.connotation: Positive. It praises someone who takes great care, though it is uncommon and can sound old-fashioned.
nuance.usage_note: Americans rarely use painstaker as a noun today. They more often say a meticulous worker, a perfectionist or a careful person, or they use the adjective painstaking, as in 'She is a painstaking researcher.' Painstaker appears in dictionaries and some older writing, so you will recognize it, but use the adjective in daily speech.

distinctions.note: A perfectionist is driven by a need for flawless results and may be stressed by them, while a painstaker is valued for steady diligence and careful work.

examples.everyday: My grandmother was a real painstaker with her quilts, and every stitch was perfect.
examples.professional: Dana is a painstaker in code review, so she catches the edge cases everyone else misses.
examples.analytical: The historian is a painstaker who rebuilds each date from primary sources instead of trusting secondary accounts.

nuance.analogy: A painstaker is like a jeweler who checks each setting under a loupe before handing over the ring.
nuance.etymology: From pains (taking pains, careful effort) plus -er, meaning one who does a thing.
common_mistakes: Using painstaker as a casual everyday noun where Americans would say perfectionist or careful worker
Stressing the second syllable, as in pain-STAY-ker

senses.definition: Of or relating to a palinode.

core.definition: Relating to a palinode, a poem or statement in which the writer formally retracts or takes back an earlier view.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on AH, the third syllable, with secondary stress on pal. The vowel is the same as in 'hot' and 'father' for most Americans, and the final -ic is short, like 'ick'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and specialized. It is used in literary criticism to describe a formal act of retraction.
nuance.usage_note: This is a specialized literary term used by scholars and critics of poetry; most Americans would never use it in conversation. In plain speech, say that the poem takes back what it said earlier, or that the writer recants. Use palinodic in academic or critical writing.

distinctions.note: Recantation is the general word for formally taking back a statement; palinodic is the literary adjective for a specific kind of poem that does so.
An apology expresses regret, while a palinode withdraws a view, often in verse, and not always with an apology.
Revision means changing a work to improve it; palinodic means explicitly retracting an earlier position.

examples.professional: In the retrospective, the author writes a palinodic note retracting last quarter's forecast, and the team appreciated the honesty.
examples.analytical: Stesichorus's famous palinode withdraws his earlier condemnation of Helen, and the palinodic turn reshapes the whole myth.

nuance.analogy: Like an author who publicly corrects an old essay, reversing its claims in a new preface.
nuance.etymology: From palinode, from Greek palinōidia 'song sung again', from palin 'again' and ōidē 'song'.
common_mistakes: Stressing the wrong syllable; it is pal-in-AH-dik, not pa-LIN-o-dik.
Confusing palinodic with palindromic; the first is about retracting a view, the second about reading the same both ways.

senses.definition: A simulated form of trading where individuals practice buying and selling securities, such as stocks or options, using virtual rather than real money.
senses.example: I practiced paper trading for three months before risking any of my savings.

core.definition: Practicing buying and selling stocks or options with simulated money instead of real money, to test a strategy.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on TRAY in trading, and the t is a flap, sounding like a soft d in American speech. The final -ing is short and light.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and practical. It suggests careful preparation rather than risk.
nuance.usage_note: In the United States, paper trading is the common term at brokerages and in finance courses, and it appears in both casual investing talk and professional settings. People say they 'paper trade' a strategy before using real money. Some brokerages call the feature a simulator or practice account instead.

distinctions.note: Backtesting runs a strategy on historical data, while paper trading tests it in live markets without real money.
