examples.professional: Your last comment was unhelpful, so can you point to the exact line that you think is wrong?
examples.analytical: The author's definition is unhelpful because it refers back to the concept it is supposed to explain.

nuance.analogy: An unhelpful answer is like a map with no roads on it: it looks like information but does not get you anywhere.
nuance.etymology: Formed from un- (not) plus helpful, from help plus -ful.
common_mistakes: Using unhelpful for a person who is simply absent; say unavailable or not around instead.
Stressing the last syllable, as in 'un-help-FULL'; the stress is on HELP.

senses.definition: Without meaning to, in an unintentional manner, not intentionally.

core.definition: Without meaning to; in a way that was not planned or intended.

pronunciation.tip: Stress is on TEN, with the same reduced ending as 'unintentional,' then a clear 'lee' at the end. Keep the last three syllables light and quick.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it removes blame from the actor.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use it in apologies and explanations, as in 'I unintentionally deleted your file.' It sounds a bit more formal than 'by accident.' In a Bible study it fits discussions of sin committed in error, where Scripture distinguishes sins done unknowingly from sins done defiantly.

distinctions.note: Accidentally is the everyday word and more common in speech; unintentionally is slightly more formal and often used in writing.
Carelessly blames the actor for a lack of care, while unintentionally only says there was no intent to cause the result.

examples.everyday: Oh no, I unintentionally left you off the group text. I'm sorry.
examples.professional: The config change unintentionally disabled logging for two services, so we rolled it back this morning.
examples.analytical: Scripture distinguishes sins committed unintentionally from those done with a high hand, so the question of intent shapes what counts as guilt.

nuance.analogy: Like a driver who drifts into another lane while glancing at a phone: the harm is real, but the aim was never there.
nuance.etymology: From un- 'not' plus intentionally, from Latin intendere 'to aim at'.
common_mistakes: Using it for a choice that was made on purpose; if you chose the action, do not say unintentionally.
Misspelling it as 'intentionaly'; keep the 'ally' ending.
nuance.biblical_note: Hebrew shegagah (שְׁגָגָה), error or inadvertence. Leviticus 4:2 (RSV) addresses a person who sins unintentionally against the LORD's commandments and provides a sin offering for it. Numbers 15:27-29 gives atonement for one who sins unintentionally, contrasted with the defiant sinner who acts with a high hand. Leviticus 5:17-19 describes guilt incurred by sinning unknowingly, which still requires a guilt offering.

senses.definition: The state or quality of being unique or one of a kind.

core.definition: The quality of being the only one of its kind, or of being different from everything else.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the second syllable, 'NEEK'. The ending '-ness' is a short, reduced syllable, so say 'nus', not 'nes' or 'nay-s'.

nuance.connotation: Positive. It suggests distinctiveness or value, though it can sound abstract in casual speech.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'uniqueness' in both everyday and academic contexts, as in 'the uniqueness of each child'. In casual talk people often say 'what makes it special' instead. A natural reply to 'What's the uniqueness of this design?' is 'It combines two techniques that nobody has tried together.'

distinctions.note: Distinctiveness refers to features that make something easy to recognize; uniqueness means there is no other like it.
Originality emphasizes being new or creative; uniqueness emphasizes being the only one of its kind.
Singularity is more formal or philosophical and can mean a unique feature or a point of extraordinary difference.

examples.everyday: I love the uniqueness of this old house, with its crooked staircase and tiny windows.
examples.professional: The main selling point is the uniqueness of our data, since no competitor has the same customer history.
examples.analytical: Christian theology affirms the uniqueness of Christ, yet it must ask how that claim relates to other faiths.

nuance.analogy: Like a thumbprint or a snowflake: each one is its own, and no other is quite the same.
nuance.etymology: From unique, plus the noun suffix -ness, meaning a state or quality.
common_mistakes: Using 'uniqueness' as a count noun with 'a uniqueness' in casual talk; 'a unique quality' or 'a unique feature' is often more natural.
Mispronouncing the ending as 'nes' instead of a reduced 'nus'.

senses.definition: Having the quality of oneness.
That concentrates power in a single body, rather than sharing it with more local bodies.
senses.example: a unitary authority

senses.definition: That contains an identity element.
Whose inverse is equal to its adjoint.
A unitary matrix or operator.

core.definition: Forming a single whole; in government, power concentrated in one central authority rather than shared with local bodies.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, and the final '-ary' sounds like 'air-ee' in careful speech, with a reduced vowel in quick speech. Avoid saying it like 'you-nit-ary' with a long vowel in the middle.

nuance.connotation: Neutral in mathematics and political science; in politics it can sound critical when it implies that power is overly centralized.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use unitary mainly in academic, legal, and political writing, and in mathematics. In news about politics, the word often describes countries like France or Japan, which are unitary states, in contrast to the federal United States. In a general conversation, a plain word like 'single' or 'centralized' is more natural.

distinctions.note: A federal system divides power between a central government and regional governments, while a unitary system keeps most power at the center.
Unified means brought together into one system, while unitary specifically emphasizes that one central authority holds the power.
Singular means one in number or unique, while unitary describes something forming one whole or one center of power.

examples.everyday: People often forget that France has a unitary system, so Paris makes most of the big decisions.
examples.professional: The consultant recommended a unitary database schema so every service reads from the same source of truth.
examples.analytical: A unitary constitution places sovereignty in one legislature, which makes local authority depend on the center's continued consent.

nuance.analogy: Like an orchestra with one conductor setting every tempo, rather than a jazz band where each musician has real say.
nuance.etymology: From Latin unitas ('oneness') with the adjectival suffix -ary.
common_mistakes: Confusing unitary with unity or with the more common word united, which describes a group that has come together.
Using unitary to mean 'unique' or 'single in number' in everyday speech, where one or only would be more natural.

senses.definition: Not polished; not brought to a polish.
senses.example: The hikers admired the rough, unpolished granite stones lying along the riverbank.

senses.definition: Deprived of polish.
senses.example: Her unpolished boots were scuffed and dull by the end of the long hike.

senses.definition: Not refined in manners or style.
senses.example: His speech was earnest but unpolished, full of awkward pauses and rough phrasing.

core.definition: Not shined or smoothed; or, of a person or work, lacking refinement, social grace, or stylistic finish.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on PAH, the second syllable. With the cot-caught merger, the vowel sounds like the one in hot. The -ished ending is one syllable, /ɪʃt/, with no separate ed.

nuance.connotation: Often mildly negative when describing manners or presentation; neutral for objects; sometimes positive when it suggests authenticity.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use unpolished for physical surfaces, like wood or silver, and for people, speeches, or drafts that lack refinement. Saying someone is unpolished is a mild criticism of manners or presentation. For a skilled but rough presenter, people may say rough around the edges. Unpolished can also praise honesty, as in an unpolished but heartfelt speech.

distinctions.note: Rough describes a surface with bumps or texture; unpolished describes a surface not shined or a person or work not refined.
Unrefined emphasizes a lack of cultivation or taste; unpolished is milder and often describes something that could still improve.

examples.everyday: His table manners are a little unpolished, but he is kind and everyone likes him.
examples.professional: The first draft of the report is unpolished, but the data in it is solid.
examples.analytical: The argument is unpolished in style, yet its account of grace is more penetrating than many finished essays.

nuance.analogy: Like a stone fresh from the riverbed: its shape is real and useful, but it has not yet been made to shine.
nuance.etymology: From un- (not) and polished, past participle of polish, from Latin polire, to smooth or make glossy.
common_mistakes: Using unpolished to mean impolite; for rude behavior, say impolite or rude.
Pronouncing the -ed ending as a separate syllable; it is /ʃt/ after sh.

senses.definition: Not reviewed.
senses.example: The new analysis is still unreviewed, so please don't cite its results in the report yet.

core.definition: Not yet examined or evaluated by someone else, especially a document, manuscript, or piece of code.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on VYOOD, the second syllable, and the -ed is silent after the d. Learners often add an extra syllable, saying ree-VYOO-ed.

nuance.connotation: Neutral in technical use; it can imply a risk of errors or lack of quality control.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use it in software, academic publishing, legal, and business writing, as in unreviewed code or an unreviewed preprint. In casual talk people say it hasn't been checked yet. Labeling something unreviewed is a way of signaling caution.

distinctions.note: Unchecked stresses that facts or accuracy have not been verified, while unreviewed stresses that no formal evaluation by others has taken place.
Unpublished means not released to the public, while unreviewed can describe a published or internal item that has not yet been formally evaluated.

examples.everyday: I'd rather not send that to the client yet, since it's still unreviewed.
examples.professional: Please don't merge the unreviewed changes into main; we need a second approval first.
examples.analytical: Scholars who cite unreviewed preprints risk building arguments on claims that have never faced critical scrutiny.

nuance.analogy: Like a letter sealed before a second reader has checked it.
nuance.etymology: From un- (not) + reviewed, from Old French reveue, from Latin revidere 'to see again'.
common_mistakes: Confusing it with unviewed, which means not watched or looked at
Adding an extra syllable and saying ree-VYOO-ed

senses.definition: Inadequate, substandard or not satisfactory.
senses.example: unsatisfactory performance

core.definition: Below an acceptable standard; not good enough for what is needed or expected.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on FAK, and the middle syllable is so reduced it nearly disappears, so say it almost as 'un-sat-iss-FAK-t'ree'. Avoid stressing the 'sat'.

nuance.connotation: Negative but fairly mild; it criticizes a result without the force of 'terrible' or 'unacceptable'.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this constantly for work, service, grades and reports: 'Your answer is unsatisfactory.' In a meeting or email it is a polite but clear criticism. For people, use 'dissatisfied' or 'unsatisfied' instead, because calling a person unsatisfactory sounds like an insult.

distinctions.note: Unsatisfactory describes a thing that falls short; unsatisfied describes a person who feels unhappy or still wants more.
Unsatisfactory is milder; unacceptable means something cannot be allowed to continue.

examples.everyday: The hotel room was clean, but the air conditioning was unsatisfactory, so we asked for a different room.
examples.professional: Your quarterly report is unsatisfactory because the forecast doesn't account for seasonal churn.
examples.analytical: Such accounts are unsatisfactory because they treat moral agency as a mere product of prior causes.

nuance.analogy: Like a meal that is edible but nowhere near what you ordered.
nuance.etymology: un- (not) + satisfactory, from Latin satisfacere 'to satisfy', from satis 'enough' + facere 'to make'.
common_mistakes: Calling a person unsatisfactory; say 'dissatisfied' or 'unsatisfied' for people's feelings.
Stressing the 'sat' syllable instead of FAK.

senses.definition: The state of being unselfish.

core.definition: The quality of putting other people's needs and wishes ahead of your own.

pronunciation.tip: The stress is on SELF, and the final -ness is a reduced 'nuhs' sound with no strong vowel. Keep the 'sh' in -ish as one clear sound.

nuance.connotation: Positive; it names a virtue admired in everyday life and in moral or religious contexts.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use unselfishness to describe a person's character, often in praise: 'Her unselfishness is why everyone trusts her.' It appears in speeches, eulogies, reviews and advice. For a single act, people more often say 'that was unselfish of you.'

distinctions.note: Selflessness is a stronger, more idealistic term often used for heroism or religious devotion.
Generosity is the readiness to give money, time or help; unselfishness is broader and describes a whole attitude of putting others first.
Altruism is a technical term in biology, psychology and ethics for concern for others' welfare, often at a cost to oneself.

examples.everyday: Her unselfishness with her time is the reason everyone at the church asks her for help.
examples.professional: Her unselfishness as a team lead, passing credit to others and mentoring junior engineers, is why we keep our best people.
examples.analytical: Unselfishness, understood as valuing others' interests as one's own, is central to Christian ethics and raises hard questions about the place of self-love.

nuance.analogy: Unselfishness is like a shared kitchen: the people who clean up without being asked are what keep it working for everyone.
nuance.etymology: From unselfish plus -ness, from self (Old English self), with the noun suffix -ness.
common_mistakes: Stressing the wrong syllable, as un-self-ISH-ness; the main stress falls on the first syllable of self.
Confusing it with unselfconsciousness, which means lack of self-awareness or embarrassment.

senses.definition: Not successfully; without success; to no avail.
senses.example: She unsuccessfully tried to reach the support line three times before giving up.

core.definition: Without achieving the intended result; in a way that fails to reach a goal.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on SES, the second-to-last main syllable. The double c is pronounced as one k plus s (suk-SES), and the final -ly is a quick, reduced 'lee'.

nuance.connotation: Negative, because it reports failure, but the tone is neutral and factual.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use it to report attempts that did not work, such as applications, negotiations, or repairs: 'I tried to renew the license online, but it failed unsuccessfully' is awkward, so use 'I tried twice to renew it online, unsuccessfully.' In casual talk, 'it didn't work' or 'it didn't pan out' is more common. A natural reply is 'Oh no, sorry to hear that.'

distinctions.note: To no avail is a more formal, somewhat literary phrase that stresses that repeated effort failed; unsuccessfully is a plain, neutral report of the result.
In vain stresses that the effort was wasted and often sounds literary; unsuccessfully is more practical and everyday.

examples.everyday: She called the landlord all week and tried unsuccessfully to get the heat fixed, so she finally sent an email.
examples.professional: Our team bid unsuccessfully on the contract, so we are revising the proposal for the next round.
examples.analytical: Several earlier theologians attempted unsuccessfully to reconcile divine foreknowledge with human freedom, and the debate continues.

nuance.analogy: Like a key that turns in the lock but never opens the door.
nuance.etymology: From un- (not) plus successfully, from Latin successus, 'outcome', from succedere, 'to follow'.
common_mistakes: Spelling: 'unsucessfully' drops a c; the word needs both the double c and the double s.
Stress: stressing the first syllable or the 'fuh'; the main stress is on SES.

senses.definition: Not able to be held or sustained, such as of an opinion or position.
senses.example: The theory of cold fusion was untenable.

senses.definition: Unfit for habitation.
senses.example: After the flood, the basement became untenable, so the family moved to a hotel.

core.definition: Impossible to defend or maintain, such as an argument, a position, or a situation that cannot continue.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on TEN, and the -able ending reduces to 'uh-bul'. Don't stress the final syllable, and don't confuse it with 'tenable' in the sense of a job or period of tenure.

nuance.connotation: Negative; it signals that a claim or situation has failed and cannot be defended or sustained.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use untenable in news, politics, legal arguments and business writing: 'the position became untenable.' It is formal and somewhat stiff for casual talk, and sounds odd in a text to a friend. A natural reply is 'Then they'll have to change the plan.'

distinctions.note: Unsustainable focuses on whether something can continue over time; untenable focuses on whether a claim or position can be defended.
Indefensible means cannot be justified morally or logically; untenable is broader and can describe a situation or a job.

examples.everyday: Working two jobs with no sleep is just untenable, so I'm cutting one of them.
examples.professional: Our current timeline is untenable, so we need to push the launch date or cut scope.
examples.analytical: Once the premise is shown to be false, the whole argument becomes untenable, however elegant its structure.

nuance.analogy: A bridge with no support underneath, which you cannot stand on for long.
nuance.etymology: From un- plus tenable, from Latin tenere, to hold.
common_mistakes: Stressing the final syllable, as in 'un-tuh-BULL'
Using it to mean unbelievable or untrue; it means cannot be defended or sustained

senses.definition: Not written.
Oral or otherwise communicated without writing.
senses.example: Our family's recipes were an unwritten tradition passed down by my grandmother.

senses.definition: Implicit or understood but not formally articulated.
senses.example: It's an unwritten rule that you lock the gate when you leave the swimming pool.

senses.definition: Containing no writing; blank.
senses.example: unwritten paper

core.definition: Not put into writing; existing as speech, custom or shared understanding rather than as a written document.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on RIT, and both the first and last syllables are weak schwas. The r is pronounced clearly, and in fast speech the t between vowels often becomes a soft flap, so it sounds close to 'uhn-RID-n'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It describes customs, rules or agreements that are understood but not recorded, and can sound positive when it refers to tradition.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'unwritten' for rules, customs and agreements that everyone knows but nobody has recorded, such as the unwritten rules of a workplace or a neighborhood. It is neutral in tone and fits both casual talk and professional writing. For spoken records use 'oral', and for a spoken business agreement use 'verbal agreement'.

distinctions.note: Oral means spoken aloud, as in oral history. Unwritten is broader and can also describe a tacit understanding that nobody has ever spoken.
Verbal means expressed in words, spoken or written, so a verbal agreement is a spoken and unwritten agreement in business settings.
Implicit means suggested without being stated directly. An unwritten rule is often known and followed, though people may state it aloud.

examples.everyday: My dad always said there's an unwritten rule that nobody leaves the table until everyone's finished.
examples.professional: We never put it in the contract, but there's an unwritten agreement that the team gets Fridays off in the summer.
examples.analytical: Legal scholars argue that unwritten constitutional principles, such as judicial independence, shape government as much as the formal text does.

nuance.analogy: An unwritten rule is like a path worn into the grass: nobody drew it on a map, but everyone walks it.
nuance.etymology: From un- (not) and written, the past participle of write, from Old English writan.
common_mistakes: Misspelling it as 'unwriten' with one t; the correct spelling has two t's.
Saying the vowel in 'writ' as a long i; it is short, like 'rit'.

unwritten.etymology: From Middle English *unwriten*, from Old English *unwriten*, *unġewriten* (“unwritten”), equivalent to *un-* + *written*.

senses.definition: Fully informed; current.
senses.example: Is Mary up to speed on the situation in Kuala Lumpur?

senses.definition: Functioning adequately.
senses.example: It may take the new hires a week or two to be brought up to speed on the system.

core.definition: Fully informed about current information or developments; caught up with what is happening.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on SPEED; the to reduces to a schwa, so it sounds like up-tuh-SPEED, and the final d is a clear, short sound. Don't say too with a long vowel.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive; implies competence and being current.
nuance.usage_note: Very common in American offices: 'Let me get you up to speed' or 'I need to get up to speed on the project.' It is used for new team members or people returning from leave. A natural reply is 'Thanks, that helps' or 'Great, what did I miss?'

distinctions.note: Informed is neutral and more formal; up to speed stresses catching up on recent developments, usually after being behind.

collocations: up to speed with the latest

examples.everyday: I was away last week, so can you bring me up to speed on the game?
examples.professional: Before the review, I'll get the new analysts up to speed on our data pipeline.
examples.analytical: A historian must get up to speed on the primary sources before offering an interpretation.

nuance.analogy: Like a runner joining a race already in progress who must match the pace of the pack.
common_mistakes: Adding an extra the, as in up to the speed
Using it for physical velocity, as in my car is up to speed

conversation.text: Can you get me up to speed on what happened while I was out?
It took the new hire a few weeks to get up to speed.
My sister brought me up to speed on the family drama.

senses.definition: Designed to be easy for an untrained user to use, with intuitive ordering of steps, consistent and logical placement of controls, etc.
senses.example: The new banking app is user-friendly, so my grandmother can pay bills herself.

core.definition: Easy for people without special training to learn and operate, with clear steps and logical controls.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress is on FREN in 'friendly,' and 'user' is lighter. The last syllable of 'friendly' is reduced, so the word sounds like 'FREN-dlee,' not 'FREN-dee-lee.'

nuance.connotation: Positive. It is a compliment about a product's design, though it can sound corporate in casual talk.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say 'it's really user-friendly' to praise apps, websites, or devices. In everyday conversation, 'easy to use' is more natural for most people. The term is for things, not for people, so you would not describe a friendly coworker as user-friendly.

distinctions.note: Intuitive means you can understand something without instructions, while user-friendly is broader and covers the overall ease of use.
'Easy to use' is plainer and more common in everyday speech, while 'user-friendly' sounds more technical and often appears in reviews or marketing.
Friendly describes a person's warmth, while user-friendly describes how easily a product can be operated.

examples.everyday: Honestly, this new banking app is pretty user-friendly, and I paid my bill in two taps.
examples.professional: We need the checkout flow to be more user-friendly before the launch next month.
examples.analytical: A design that is user-friendly is not merely pleasant to look at; it anticipates the user's mental model and reduces the errors that arise when the two diverge.

nuance.analogy: Like a well-marked trail: you can follow it without a map, because each turn is clear.
nuance.etymology: A compound of 'user' (from 'use') and 'friendly' (from Old English); it has been used in computing since about the 1970s.
common_mistakes: Writing 'user friendly' without a hyphen when it comes before a noun; the hyphen is standard in that position.
Saying 'a user-friendly person' to mean someone who is warm or approachable; the term is for products or systems.

senses.definition: A device that uses suction, and often agitation, in order to remove dirt and other debris from carpets and hard floors.
senses.example: She ran the vacuum cleaner over the carpet before the guests arrived.

senses.definition: The buttocks or anus.
senses.example: He landed hard on his vacuum cleaner after slipping on the icy steps.

core.definition: An electric appliance that sucks up dirt, dust, and debris from carpets and hard floors.

pronunciation.tip: Both words have a stressed syllable: VAK in vacuum and KLEE in cleaner. The word vacuum is pronounced 'VAK-yoom,' not 'VAK-yoo-um,' and the final r in cleaner is pronounced as a retroflex r.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is an everyday household word.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say vacuum cleaner or just vacuum, as in I need to vacuum the living room. Vacuum is also a verb in everyday American English. The British word hoover is mainly a brand name, so use vacuum cleaner in the United States. The slang sense of buttocks is a crude joke that should be avoided in polite conversation.

distinctions.note: Vacuum alone can be a verb meaning to clean with a vacuum cleaner or a noun meaning empty space, so use vacuum cleaner for the appliance.
A broom sweeps dirt with bristles, while a vacuum cleaner uses suction to pull dirt into a bag or canister.

examples.everyday: Can you run the vacuum cleaner before the guests get here?
examples.professional: Facilities ordered two new vacuum cleaners for the office floors, since the old ones keep clogging.
examples.analytical: The vacuum cleaner transformed domestic labor, and its history shows how household technology reshaped expectations about housework.

nuance.analogy: A vacuum cleaner is like a giant straw that breathes in dirt instead of drinking a drink.
nuance.etymology: Vacuum is from Latin vacuus, empty; cleaner comes from clean plus the agent suffix -er.
common_mistakes: Saying hoover for vacuum cleaner in American English; hoover is a British brand-name term.
Pronouncing vacuum as VAK-yoo-um with a third syllable; the usual American pronunciation is two syllables, VAK-yoom.

senses.definition: The state, condition or habits of a valetudinarian; a state of feeble health; infirmity.

core.definition: A state of habitual concern with one's health, or a condition of weak or sickly health.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on NAIR, the third-from-last syllable, and the word has five syllables before the ending. Americans say the middle syllables quickly with reduced vowels, and the final -ism is a clear 'izm'.

nuance.connotation: Negative or slightly mocking, since it describes an excessive or anxious focus on one's health.
nuance.usage_note: Americans rarely use this word in conversation. It appears in literature, medical history or essays about illness and hypochondria. In everyday speech, people say 'hypochondria' or just 'always worrying about their health.'

distinctions.note: Hypochondria is an anxious belief that one is seriously ill, while valetudinarianism is a broader habit of invalid-like self-care, often with real frailty.
Infirmity is a general word for physical weakness, while valetudinarianism focuses on the habits and attitudes of a person preoccupied with health.

examples.professional: In the clinical history, the patient's valetudinarianism was documented as a lifelong pattern of avoiding exertion.
examples.analytical: Victorian novels often treat valetudinarianism as a social performance, using illness to gain attention and control within the household.

nuance.analogy: Valetudinarianism is like a car that stays in the garage with the hood up, always being checked but seldom driven.
nuance.etymology: From Latin valetudinarius, 'sickly', from valetudo, 'state of health', from valere, 'to be strong'.
common_mistakes: Confusing it with valediction, which is a farewell.
Stressing the wrong syllable; the main stress is on NAIR, not on the first syllable.

senses.definition: To render valid.
senses.example: The notary's stamp will validate the lease, making it legally binding.

senses.definition: To check or prove the validity of; verify.
senses.example: Our team will validate the model against a held-out dataset before deployment.

senses.definition: To have its validity successfully proven.
senses.example: The data file cannot be imported because it doesn't validate.

core.definition: To confirm that something is correct, legitimate, or accurate, often by checking evidence or using a test.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable. Americans say the 'ih' quickly, and the last syllable has a clear 'ayt' like 'date'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive. It suggests careful checking that gives confidence. In psychology or emotional contexts it can mean acknowledging someone's feelings as reasonable.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say 'validate' at work when testing a result, checking a form, or confirming a password. In everyday conversation it can mean that someone accepts your feelings, as in 'She validated my feelings.' In professional talk, 'validate the data' is common, and it is slightly more formal than 'check'.

distinctions.note: 'Verify' means to confirm that something is true. 'Validate' often means to confirm that something is correct or fit for its purpose.
'Confirm' is broad and everyday. 'Validate' is more technical and suggests a formal check against a standard.

examples.everyday: Can you validate my parking ticket before you leave?
examples.professional: Before we ship the report, we need to validate the numbers against last quarter's totals.
examples.analytical: A theory is not validated merely by evidence that fits it; it must also survive attempts to refute it.

nuance.analogy: Validating a result is like checking a recipe by tasting the finished dish against the original goal.
nuance.etymology: From valid, from Latin validus 'strong, effective'.
common_mistakes: Using 'validate' to mean 'make valid' in every context; the meaning depends on the object.
Stressing the second syllable instead of the first.

validate.etymology: Medieval Latin *validātus* (“to validate”) (perhaps through Middle French *valider*), the perfect passive participle of *validō* (see *-ate*), from *validus* + *-ō*.

senses.definition: The person or people at the forefront of a group or movement.
The leading units at the front of an army or fleet.
senses.example: The vanguard of the army crossed the river at dawn while the main force waited behind.

core.definition: The people or group at the front of a movement, field, or change, leading the way for others.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the first syllable, and the second syllable is a clear, short gard, with the r pronounced. Do not say van-GARD.

nuance.connotation: Positive. It suggests bravery, innovation, and leadership at the front of change.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use vanguard mostly in news, writing, and formal speech about movements, technologies, or social change. It is rarely used in casual conversation. Typical phrases are in the vanguard of and the vanguard of a movement. A simpler everyday alternative is leaders or pioneers.

distinctions.note: A pioneer is someone who first opens new ground, while a vanguard is a group that leads the way at the front of change.
Leader is general and everyday, while vanguard suggests a group at the front of a movement or change.
Avant-garde refers mainly to experimental art, literature, or music, while vanguard covers any movement or field.

examples.everyday: Our team has been in the vanguard of switching to electric cars at work for two years.
examples.professional: Our data platform team has been in the vanguard of adopting real-time streaming across the company.
examples.analytical: Thinkers who defended individual conscience were often the vanguard of later political reform.

nuance.analogy: Like the lead runners in a marathon, who set the pace and show the way while the rest of the field follows.
nuance.etymology: From Old French avantgarde, meaning advance guard, from avant (before) and garde (guard).
common_mistakes: Using vanguard as a verb; it is a noun, so say lead or be at the vanguard.
Saying the vanguard for every leader; it usually refers to a group at the front of a movement.

vanguard.etymology: From Middle English *vandgard,vaunte garde,vaunt garde,wantgard*, from *advaunte-garde*, *avauntgard* with aphesis, from Old French *avangarde,avant-garde,avantgarde*, from *avant* (“before; in front”) + *garde* (“guard”).

senses.definition: A kind of variable, used by a fragment shader, that interpolates values across a primitive, so as to produce gradient effects etc.
senses.example: The fragment shader reads each varying and blends the colors smoothly across the triangle.

core.definition: In computer graphics, a shader variable passed from the vertex stage to the fragment stage and interpolated across a primitive to create smooth gradient effects.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the first syllable, VAIR, and the r is pronounced in General American. Non-native speakers often stress the second syllable or drop the r, so keep the ending short and light.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a precise technical term with no emotional charge outside graphics programming.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this sense mainly among graphics programmers, game developers and shader authors, often in the plural as 'varyings' in older GLSL code. In newer shader languages the same idea is handled by in and out qualifiers, so you may hear people say 'interpolated inputs' instead. Outside technical settings the everyday word is 'changing' or 'different'.

distinctions.note: A uniform variable is the same for every vertex or fragment in a draw call, while a varying is interpolated and differs across the surface.
An attribute is per-vertex input to the vertex shader, while a varying is the output that carries interpolated values into the fragment shader.
Variable is the general programming term for any named storage; varying is a specific shader qualifier for values that interpolate across a surface.

collocations: pass a varying to the fragment shader

examples.everyday: My coworker keeps talking about shader varyings, but I have no idea what they are.
examples.professional: We declare a varying for the normal vector so the lighting looks smooth across each triangle.
examples.analytical: The rasterizer interpolates each varying, so the value at every fragment is a weighted blend of the vertex outputs, which is why the gradient looks continuous.

nuance.analogy: A varying is like a paint gradient across a wall: the corners are set at specific colors, and everything in between is blended smoothly.
nuance.etymology: From the English verb 'vary', from Latin variare, to change, from varius, diverse.
common_mistakes: Stressing the second syllable, as in 'vuh-RY-ing' instead of 'VAIR-ee-ing'.
Confusing varying with various, which means several different kinds, not something changing continuously.

senses.definition: Pertaining to a prophet; prophetic, oracular.
senses.example: Her vatic warnings about the flood sounded mad at the time but proved entirely accurate.

core.definition: Of or relating to a prophet; having the manner of a prophet or oracle, especially in speaking about the future.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, VAT. The second syllable is a short 'ih,' and the final -ic is 'ik,' not 'eek.'

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive; it often suggests a dignified or mysterious authority.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'vatic' mostly in literary criticism, poetry, religious writing, or formal essays. It is rare in speech. People more often say 'prophetic' or 'oracular' in everyday talk.

distinctions.note: Prophetic is common and can describe any accurate prediction; vatic suggests a more formal or inspired, almost oracular style.
Oracular suggests obscure or authoritative pronouncements; vatic emphasizes the prophetic role or voice.

examples.everyday: My grandfather has a vatic way of saying things, as if he already knew how the game would end.
examples.professional: The speaker's vatic tone made the strategy memo feel more like a warning than a plan.
examples.analytical: Blake's vatic poems adopt the voice of the prophet, claiming to reveal what ordinary perception cannot see.

nuance.analogy: Like a weather forecaster speaking with the authority of a seer, not just reading data.
nuance.etymology: From Latin 'vaticus,' prophetic, from 'vates,' seer or prophet.
common_mistakes: Using 'vatic' for 'vacation' or confusing it with 'static' in speech.
Pronouncing the final syllable as 'eek' instead of 'ik.'

senses.definition: Of, pertaining to, or characteristic of bats.

core.definition: Of, relating to, or characteristic of bats.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the third syllable, TIL. Keep the r in the middle syllable and reduce the final syllables to a quick schwa sound.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a precise zoological or descriptive term with no emotional charge.
nuance.usage_note: This is a rare, learned adjective that appears mainly in scientific writing, natural history, or literary description. Americans would more often say bat-like or describe the animal directly. Using it in conversation can sound showy, though it is accurate.

distinctions.note: Bat-like is the everyday American phrase and is far more common. Vespertilian is a specialized, learned synonym.

examples.everyday: The shapes flitting over the lake at dusk were vespertilian, so we knew they were bats.
examples.professional: The field guide lists the vespertilian species we recorded during the county survey.
examples.analytical: The novel's vespertilian imagery of the dark, circling night links the narrator's fear to the predator's stealth.

nuance.analogy: Like the word lupine for wolves, vespertilian is a specialized label that belongs in the naturalist's notebook.
nuance.etymology: From Latin vespertilio, bat, from vesper, evening.
common_mistakes: Using it as a general word for nocturnal animals instead of only bats.
Stressing the wrong syllable as vess-PER-tilian.

senses.definition: A person who lives in, or comes from, a village.
A worker unit.
senses.example: In the strategy game, each villager gathers wood or food for your growing town.

core.definition: A person who lives in a village or comes from one.

pronunciation.tip: The stress is on VIL, and the final -er is a reduced, r-colored vowel. The middle syllable is weak, so say 'VIL-ij-er' with the final syllable very light.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It describes a person by place of residence, and it can sound slightly old-fashioned or rustic depending on context.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use villager for people from small rural places, often in news stories, fairy tales, or descriptions of local life. In most of the US people say 'townspeople' or 'locals' for residents of a small place. The word can also refer to the people of a village in fantasy or historical contexts, as in movies and novels.

distinctions.note: A local is someone who lives in or is familiar with a place, which can apply to any size of town or city, while villager specifically refers to a village.
A townsperson lives in a town, while a villager lives in a smaller community.

collocations: the villagers of a remote village

examples.everyday: The villagers here all know each other, so the diner owner remembered my name after one visit.
examples.professional: Our field team interviewed villagers about how the new water filter has changed their daily routine.
examples.analytical: In the parable, the villagers represent a community whose judgments depend more on rumor than on evidence.

nuance.analogy: A villager is like a regular at a neighborhood coffee shop: everyone knows their face and their story.
nuance.etymology: From village plus the suffix -er, 'one who lives in'.
common_mistakes: Using villager for a person from a large town or city, which sounds wrong to Americans.
Confusing the word with 'village people' in a way that sounds like a band name or a stereotype.

senses.definition: Promoting or producing vindication.
Promoting or producing retribution or punishment.

core.definition: Serving to vindicate; showing that someone or something was justified, or proving someone's claim right.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on DIK. The 'uh' is a reduced vowel, and the ending -ory is pronounced 'or-ee' in General American, with the r sound audible.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive. It describes actions or statements that clear a name or prove a point.
nuance.usage_note: This is a formal or academic word. Americans more often say 'justifying' or 'vindicating' as verbs, or 'proving someone right' in speech. The word appears in legal, literary, and scholarly writing.

distinctions.note: Punitive means meant to punish. Vindicatory means meant to clear or prove right, although it can also refer to rightful retribution in older usage.
Justificatory emphasizes giving reasons for an action. Vindicatory emphasizes proving that someone was right or cleared of blame.

examples.everyday: The letter from the company was a vindicatory note that cleared my brother's name.
examples.professional: The internal audit issued a vindicatory summary showing that the team's data pipeline was sound.
examples.analytical: The essay's vindicatory tone defends the author's earlier thesis against decades of critical dismissal.

nuance.analogy: A vindicatory verdict is like a court ruling that clears a defendant's name in public.
nuance.etymology: From Latin vindicare, 'to claim, avenge', through the stem of vindication.
common_mistakes: Confusing vindicatory with vindictive, which describes a desire for revenge.
Using the adjective when a verb such as 'vindicate' is more natural in speech.

senses.definition: In a vivid manner.

core.definition: In a way that produces clear, strong, sharp mental images or intense feelings.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, VIV. The first vowel is short, as in 'bit', not a long 'eye' sound, and the middle syllable is reduced to a quick 'id'.

nuance.connotation: Positive or neutral. It usually praises clarity and detail, though it can describe painful memories or disturbing images.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this word often in everyday speech, especially with verbs like 'remember' and 'picture'. People say 'I remember it vividly' to describe a clear memory, and they say 'it was vividly colored' to describe bright visuals. A natural reply is to share your own memory or ask a follow-up question.

distinctions.note: Clearly focuses on being easy to see, hear, or understand. Vividly focuses on intensity and emotional impact.
Graphically emphasizes explicit or disturbing detail, often gory. Vividly can be positive and does not imply shock.

examples.everyday: I remember that summer vividly, the smell of the lake and the sound of the screen door.
examples.professional: The dashboard shows the latency spike vividly, so the team can see exactly when the outage began.
examples.analytical: Dostoevsky renders guilt so vividly that the reader begins to feel the narrator's suffocation.

nuance.analogy: Like a photo with the contrast turned all the way up: every edge and color stands out sharply.
nuance.etymology: From vivid, from Latin vividus, 'lively, vigorous', from vivere, 'to live'.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the first vowel as a long 'eye' sound (VY-vid-lee) instead of a short 'i'.
Using vividly for a person's energetic manner; vivaciously is the better word for that.

senses.definition: Of or pertaining to a vocation.
senses.example: She enrolled in a vocational program to train as an electrician after high school.

senses.definition: That provides a special skill rather than academic knowledge.
senses.example: vocational scheme

core.definition: Relating to a job or trade, especially one that needs practical skills rather than academic study.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the syllable KAY. The ending '-tional' is pronounced 'shuh-nuhl,' not 'tee-on-al,' and the word is different from 'vocal'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to slightly positive. It describes practical training, though some people may see it as less prestigious than an academic degree.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'vocational' in education and career talk, as in 'vocational training' or 'vocational programs.' It is common in school policy, community college discussions and workforce development. People often prefer 'trade' or 'technical' for specific jobs like plumbing or electrical work.

distinctions.note: Professional often means requiring advanced education or license, such as law or medicine, while vocational means practical, skills-based training.
Academic refers to theoretical study and scholarship, while vocational refers to job-focused training.
Occupational is about jobs in general, including health and safety, as in occupational therapy, while vocational focuses on training for a trade.

examples.everyday: My cousin took a vocational program after high school and now works as an electrician.
examples.professional: We want to recruit more candidates from vocational programs for our technician roles.
examples.analytical: Vocational education prepares students for specific occupations, whereas liberal education aims at broad intellectual formation.

nuance.analogy: Vocational training is like learning to fix a car in the garage rather than reading about engines in a classroom.
nuance.etymology: From Late Latin vocationalis, from vocatio (a calling), from vocare (to call).
common_mistakes: Confusing vocational with vocal, which means relating to the voice.
Stressing the wrong syllable, such as 'vo-ca-TION-al' instead of 'voh-KAY-shuh-nuhl.'

senses.definition: A whirlwind, whirlpool, or similarly moving matter in the form of a spiral or column.
senses.example: The dust devil became a vortex that spun leaves and paper across the parking lot.

senses.definition: Anything that involves constant violent or chaotic activity around some center.
senses.example: The city council meetings had become a vortex of constant shouting and chaos.

senses.definition: Anything that inevitably draws surrounding things into its current.
senses.example: Once the rumor started, the whole office got pulled into its vortex.

senses.definition: A group of vultures or buzzards.
senses.example: A vortex of vultures circled above the dry canyon as the sun went down.

senses.definition: Any of numerous species of small Turbellaria belonging to Vortex and allied genera.
senses.example: Under the microscope, the student identified a vortex, a small flatworm from the pond sample.

senses.definition: (historical) A supposed collection of particles of very subtle matter, endowed with a rapid rotary motion around an axis which was also the axis of a sun or planet; part of a Cartesian theory accounting for the formation of the universe, and the movements of the bodies composing it.
senses.example: Descartes proposed that a vortex of subtle matter carried the planets around the sun.
senses.label: historical

senses.definition: To mix using a vortex mixer.
senses.example: Before measuring, the chemist vortexed the sample for thirty seconds in the mixer.

core.definition: A whirling mass of air, water or other fluid moving in a spiral, or a situation that pulls things into chaos.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable. The vowel in 'vor' is the 'or' sound of 'core' or 'door', so it is not 'vort' with an 'ah'. The final 'x' is pronounced like 'ks'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral in physics and weather; negative when used figuratively for a situation that draws people into trouble.
nuance.usage_note: In everyday American speech, people use 'vortex' for swirling water or wind, and in news and business for a bad situation that pulls people in, such as 'a vortex of debt'. In casual talk, 'whirlpool' or 'tornado' may be used instead. Figurative use is common in journalism.

distinctions.note: A whirlpool is a swirling current of water, while a vortex can be air, water or a figurative situation.
A tornado is a violent column of air from a storm; a vortex is a more general spinning motion.
An eddy is a small local swirl, usually in a stream; a vortex is often larger or more intense.

examples.everyday: The water drained out of the sink in a fast vortex, like a little whirlpool.
examples.professional: Our project got pulled into a vortex of scope changes and urgent requests, so we lost two weeks.
examples.analytical: Her argument falls into a vortex of self-reference, where each claim depends on the one it is supposed to support.

nuance.analogy: A vortex is like a spinning drain that pulls everything nearby toward its center.
nuance.etymology: From Latin vortex, 'whirlpool', from vertere, 'to turn'.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the middle as 'vert-ex' with a strong 'r' sound that is too heavy; keep the American 'r' light.
Using 'vortex' for a single small wave, where 'ripple' is more natural.

senses.definition: To get married.

core.definition: To get married; to take part in a wedding by walking up the center aisle of a church or hall to the altar.

pronunciation.tip: Aisle sounds like 'ile', because the s is silent. Reduce the to thuh before a consonant and thee before a vowel, and link the words smoothly.

nuance.connotation: Positive; it describes a happy and important life event.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this phrase for getting married, often with a playful or sentimental tone. The phrase may refer literally to the wedding procession, such as walking down the aisle with the bride's father. Neutral alternatives are get married, and informal ones are tie the knot.

distinctions.note: Get married is neutral and literal; walk down the aisle is warmer and refers to the wedding ceremony.
Tie the knot is informal and common in conversation; walk down the aisle is more traditional.
Walk up the aisle is uncommon; walk down the aisle is the standard phrase in American weddings.

collocations: walk down the aisle with her father
never thought I'd walk down the aisle

examples.everyday: My sister is finally walking down the aisle in June.
examples.professional: HR asked whether the new leave policy covers employees who are walking down the aisle this summer.
examples.analytical: Anthropologists often describe the wedding procession as a ritual through which the couple's social status is publicly changed as they walk down the aisle.

nuance.analogy: The aisle is like a bridge from the single life to married life, and walking across it marks the change.
common_mistakes: Saying walk to the aisle; the standard phrase is walk down the aisle.
Pronouncing aisle with a sounded s, as in 'ai-sul'; the s is silent.

senses.definition: A proponent of war or military intrusiveness.
senses.example: The senator was a known war hawk who pushed for military action abroad.

senses.definition: (dated) An eagle.
senses.example: In the old naturalist book, the author described a war hawk soaring above the cliffs.
senses.label: dated

core.definition: A person who strongly favors military action or aggressive foreign policy, and who often pushes for war rather than negotiation.

pronunciation.tip: Stress WAR in this compound noun, with the second word 'hawk' weaker. The 'aw' in 'hawk' is the same vowel as 'talk,' not an 'ah' sound.

nuance.connotation: Negative when used by critics, though a person may call themselves a hawk to sound firm and realistic.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'war hawk' and 'hawk' in news and political discussion, mainly about foreign policy, defense spending, and military intervention. The opposite label is 'dove.' Calling someone a war hawk is a sharp political criticism, so use it with care.

distinctions.note: Hawk can be used more broadly, for example for a strict monetary policy supporter, while war hawk specifically refers to military conflict.
Warmonger is much stronger and implies someone who deliberately stirs up war, while war hawk describes a policy stance.

examples.everyday: My brother-in-law is a total war hawk when it comes to foreign policy.
examples.professional: The board's war hawks want to cut prices and crush the competitor, even though it will hurt us long term.
examples.analytical: Such war hawks treat diplomacy as a failure of nerve rather than a legitimate tool of statecraft.

nuance.analogy: A war hawk is like a referee who calls every foul as a reason to start the fight, rather than to restore the game.
nuance.etymology: Compound of 'war' and 'hawk,' the bird of prey used as an image of aggression.
common_mistakes: Stressing 'hawk' equally with 'war,' which sounds unnatural in American speech.
Saying 'war hawk' for a person who only wants strong defense, when 'hawk' or 'defense hawk' is more precise.

senses.definition: The quality of being weighty.

core.definition: The quality of being important, serious or influential in a way that deserves careful attention.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable. The middle syllable is a short 'tin', not 'teen', and the ending is a reduced 'us'.

nuance.connotation: Positive or neutral. It suggests gravity and seriousness that commands respect.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use weightiness mainly for ideas, decisions and responsibilities, usually in writing or formal speeches. In conversation they more often say 'how serious it is' or 'how important it is'. It can sound stiff in casual speech.

distinctions.note: Importance is neutral and everyday; weightiness suggests a grave, serious kind of importance that carries moral or intellectual gravity.
Gravity can mean seriousness or physical pull; weightiness is narrower and focuses on the significance a matter carries.

examples.everyday: I know this decision is a big one, and I appreciate you taking its weightiness seriously.
examples.professional: The board recognized the weightiness of the compliance decision and asked for a written memo before Friday.
examples.analytical: The weightiness of moral obligation in Kant's ethics stems from its unconditional character, which no consequence can cancel.

nuance.analogy: Like a stone set on one side of a scale, the matter tips everything else toward it.
nuance.etymology: From weighty, from weight, with the suffix -ness.
common_mistakes: Spelling it 'weightyness' with an extra y; the noun drops the y from weighty.
Using it for physical heaviness in everyday talk; say 'heaviness' instead.
Pronouncing the middle syllable like 'teen'.

senses.definition: The state or quality of being weird.
The result or product of being weird.
senses.example: The weirdness of the hotel's silent elevator made everyone in our group laugh nervously.

core.definition: The quality of being strange or unusual, or an odd thing that happens or someone does.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable. Move directly from the d to the n with no extra vowel between them, and keep the ending reduced.

nuance.connotation: Negative to neutral. It can be playful when describing a pleasant strangeness.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use weirdness for an odd atmosphere, a strange feeling or a bizarre pattern, as in 'the weirdness of the day.' In everyday talk they more often say 'that was weird.' Describing a person's weirdness can sound dismissive, so 'eccentricity' is the kinder word.

distinctions.note: Strangeness is more neutral and general; weirdness adds an informal sense of oddness that often feels unsettling or funny.
Eccentricity is a kinder, somewhat formal word for harmless oddness in a person; weirdness can sound like criticism.

examples.everyday: There was a weirdness to the party; everyone kept whispering and nobody would say why.
examples.professional: The weirdness in the sensor logs disappeared after we updated the firmware on the gateway.
examples.analytical: The weirdness of faith, which asks us to trust what we cannot see, is central to Kierkegaard's account of the leap.

nuance.analogy: Like a painting hung slightly crooked, the weirdness is hard to name but impossible to ignore.
nuance.etymology: From weird, with the suffix -ness.
common_mistakes: Dropping the d and writing 'weirness'.
Using weirdness to mean a person; say weirdo or eccentric person for a person.
Stressing the wrong syllable or lengthening the first vowel into 'weird-ness' with a long e.

what's-the-best-number-to-reach-you.phonetic: /ˌwʌts ðə ˌbɛst ˌnʌmbɚ tu ˈɹitʃ ju/

senses.definition: Asking which phone number to use to call someone back.

core.definition: A question asking which phone number is the best one to use when you need to call someone back.

pronunciation.respelling: wuts thuh best NUM-ber too REECH yoo
pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on REACH in this phrase, and 'to' is reduced to 'tuh' before a consonant. Americans link 'reach you' smoothly, so it sounds like 'REE-chuh'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and polite. It is a practical question that sounds helpful in a business or service context.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say this at the end of a call, at a doctor's office, or when a contractor or recruiter needs a callback. A natural answer gives a number and a time, such as 'Cell is best, or call the office after five.' The phrase is standard in professional and everyday phone calls; 'What's the best number to call you back on?' is also common.

distinctions.note: 'What's your phone number?' asks for any number, while 'What's the best number to reach you?' asks which one to use, implying you have more than one.

distinctions.vs: What's the best way to reach you?
distinctions.note: 'What's the best way to reach you?' includes email, text, or other channels, while this phrase focuses specifically on a phone number.

collocations: the best number to reach you
what's the best number to call
call you back at the number
a good number to reach you

examples.everyday: Thanks for calling the dentist back. What's the best number to reach you if we need to reschedule?
examples.professional: Thanks for the interview, Dana. What's the best number to reach you before Thursday so we can set up the panel?
examples.analytical: The question 'What's the best number to reach you?' reveals that a phone number is not a fixed identity but a contextual channel chosen for convenience.

nuance.analogy: It is like asking which door to knock on when you want to find someone at home.
common_mistakes: Saying 'the best number for reaching you' is understandable but less natural than 'to reach you'.
Forgetting that 'number' is countable, so 'the best numbers' would be wrong when you mean one.

conversation.text: What's the best number to reach you if we get disconnected?

senses.definition: One who wheedles; a sweet talker.

core.definition: A person who coaxes, flatters or pesters someone persistently to get what they want.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable and make the middle sound a quick 'dl' that blends into the final 'er'. The ending is a reduced vowel, so say 'ler' softly, not 'lee-er'.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It suggests someone who uses sweet talk in a manipulative or insincere way.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'wheedler' rarely, mainly in literary writing or in a playful description of a child or a salesperson who keeps asking. It is closely tied to the verb 'wheedle', which is more common. Calling someone a wheedler in conversation can sound critical, so use it with care.

distinctions.note: A flatterer praises someone to please them or gain favor, while a wheedler uses coaxing and persistence to get a specific thing.
A cajoler persuades with gentle, playful charm, while a wheedler suggests more persistent and less sincere pressure.

examples.everyday: My little brother is a real wheedler, always asking for one more cookie.
examples.professional: A good negotiator is not a wheedler; they earn trust with facts rather than flattery.
examples.analytical: Socrates confronts the wheedler, the sophist whose flattering words win assent without truth.

nuance.analogy: A wheedler is like a cat that rubs against your leg until you give it what it wants.
nuance.etymology: From the verb wheedle, of uncertain origin, perhaps from German wedeln, meaning to wag the tail.
common_mistakes: Confusing 'wheedler' with 'wheeler', which is a different word about wheels.
Using it as a verb, when 'wheedle' is the verb form.

senses.definition: The state or condition of being whiny.

core.definition: The quality of sounding high, thin, and complaining, or of being prone to whining.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable: WY-nee-nus. The -ness ends with a reduced vowel, so say 'nus', not 'nes'. The middle vowel is a quick 'ih' or 'ee'.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It describes an irritating, self-pitying quality in a voice or attitude.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'whininess' when describing a person's voice or tone, like 'the whininess in her voice.' It is casual and can be insulting. In writing or reviews, 'petulance' or 'peevishness' sounds more polished.

distinctions.note: Peevishness is more formal and suggests irritable bad temper; whininess is a high, complaining quality of voice or manner.
Complaining is the act; whininess is the tone or quality of that complaining.
Petulance suggests a childish sulky anger; whininess suggests a more persistent, high-pitched complaint.

examples.everyday: I'm tired of the whininess in your voice every time we talk about chores.
examples.professional: The whininess in the status updates made the project feel worse than it was.
examples.analytical: The essay's whininess undermines its argument, because the reader hears grievance more than reasoning.

nuance.analogy: Whininess is like a fly buzzing near your ear: thin, persistent, and hard to ignore.
nuance.etymology: Formed from whiny with the suffix -ness, from whine.
common_mistakes: Spelling it 'whinyness'; the y changes to i before -ness.
Using it for a loud voice; whininess is specifically about a high, complaining tone.

senses.definition: Producing or resembling a whisper.
senses.example: She spoke in a whispery voice so the sleeping baby would not wake up.

core.definition: Sounding like a whisper; soft, breathy and barely audible.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, and the final -y is a light 'ee' sound. Keep the middle syllable reduced to 'puh' rather than a full vowel.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive; it usually describes a soft, intimate or mysterious voice or sound, though it can sound thin when describing a person's speech.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use whispery mostly to describe a voice, laugh or sound that is breathy and quiet, as in 'she has a whispery voice on the phone.' It is descriptive and natural in both conversation and writing. In everyday speech, people also say breathy or soft.

distinctions.note: Breathy describes a voice with audible air in it, a physical quality of production; whispery describes a sound that resembles a whisper, whether or not air is audible.
Hushed describes a quiet atmosphere, often because people are trying to be silent, while whispery describes the sound itself.

examples.everyday: Her voice got really whispery on the phone, so I had to turn the volume all the way up.
examples.professional: The narrator's whispery delivery made the safety video hard to follow in the training room.
examples.analytical: The poem's whispery syntax, with its half-finished clauses, asks the reader to lean in rather than be told.

nuance.analogy: Like a candle flame that flickers without a sound.
nuance.etymology: From whisper plus the suffix -y; whisper comes from Old English hwisprian.
common_mistakes: Using whispering as an adjective for a quality of voice; say 'a whispery voice', since 'a whispering voice' suggests the speaker is whispering right now.
Pronouncing the final -y as 'eye' instead of 'ee'.

senses.definition: Magic derived from good or benign forces, as distinct from evil or malevolent forces; or magic performed with the intention of doing good or giving aid.
senses.example: The villagers asked the healer for white magic to protect their harvest from the storm.

core.definition: Magic believed to use good or benevolent forces, meant to heal, protect or help people, as opposed to harmful black magic.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable of 'magic,' MAJ-ik, not on the second. The 'g' is pronounced like the 'j' in 'judge,' and the final syllable is short, like 'ick' without the k sound stretched out.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to negative depending on context. Fantasy writers and folklorists use it casually, while religious Americans often reject the idea of any magic as spiritually dangerous.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'white magic' mostly in fantasy novels, games, folklore, and discussions of the occult. Among Christians, many would object that magic of any color is condemned in Scripture, so the term can start a debate in church settings. In everyday talk, 'magic' alone is the normal word, and 'white magic' sounds like a deliberate contrast with black magic.

distinctions.note: Black magic is used for harmful or evil magic, while white magic is used for benevolent or protective magic.
Witchcraft is a broader term for practices associated with witches, often with pagan or folk associations, and it is frequently negative.
A miracle is an act of God, understood by believers as beyond human control, while white magic is a supposed human technique for using spiritual forces.

examples.everyday: My daughter loves fantasy novels, and her favorite characters use white magic to heal their friends.
examples.professional: Our game designers separated the spell list into white magic for healing and buffs, and black magic for damage and curses.
examples.analytical: Some medieval writers distinguished benign natural magic from demonic practice, but many theologians condemned both as attempts to control spiritual powers outside God's will.

nuance.analogy: Like a flashlight that people try to use for good or ill: the tool is the same, and the intent defines the color.
nuance.etymology: White from Old English hwīt; magic from Middle English magik, from Latin magice, from Greek magikē, the art of the magoi.
common_mistakes: Stressing the second syllable of 'magic'; the American stress is MAJ-ik.
Using 'white magic' in a religious conversation without realizing many Christians consider all magic forbidden.
nuance.biblical_note: Scripture does not divide magic into white and black; it condemns the practices themselves. The Hebrew word kāšap (sorcery, practice of magic) appears in Deuteronomy 18:10-12 (RSV), which forbids Israel to practice divination, sorcery, or consulting the dead. In the New Testament, the Greek word mageia (magic, sorcery) appears in Acts 8:9-24, where Simon of Samaria is rebuked for trying to buy spiritual power, and Acts 19:19 describes Ephesian converts burning their magic books. Galatians 5:20 also lists sorcery (pharmakeia) among works of the flesh.

senses.definition: A witty or sarcastic comment or quip.
senses.example: He ended the tense meeting with a wisecrack about the coffee, and everyone laughed.

senses.definition: To make a sarcastic, flippant, or sardonic comment.
senses.example: Whenever the manager got nervous, Tom would wisecrack about the budget to lighten the mood.

core.definition: A quick, clever remark, often sarcastic, meant to be funny.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable. Pronounce the r in 'crack' because American English is rhotic, and use the short a of 'cat'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to mildly negative; the remark is witty but often sarcastic and sometimes at someone's expense.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use wisecrack for a quick, often sarcastic joke in casual talk, meetings, or among friends. 'Cut the wisecracks' is a mild request to get serious. The word is not used for a carefully written joke or a serious comment.

distinctions.note: A joke is any humorous story or remark; a wisecrack is a quick, sharp remark, often sarcastic.
A pun plays on the double meaning of words; a wisecrack may include a pun but is defined by its quick, cutting humor.

examples.everyday: Every time the game went into overtime, Dan made some wisecrack about his bad knees.
examples.professional: Please keep the wisecracks out of the client call, since they are taking this demo seriously.
examples.analytical: Much of Wilde's wit survives in quotable form, but a wisecrack alone rarely reveals the argument beneath it.

nuance.analogy: A wisecrack is a verbal dart: quick, sharp, and aimed at something.
nuance.etymology: Compound of wise (clever) and crack (a smart remark or joke).
common_mistakes: Writing it as two words, 'wise crack'
Using wisecrack for a serious or formal comment

senses.definition: The practice of witches; magic, sorcery, or the use of supernatural powers to influence or predict events.
senses.example: Wiccans believe in a modernized form of witchcraft.

senses.definition: Black magic; the use of witchcraft for evil means.
senses.example: The Bible warns against the use of witchcraft and sorcery.

senses.definition: Something, such as an advanced technology, that seems almost magical.
senses.example: Our engineers joked that the new compression algorithm was pure witchcraft.

senses.definition: An irresistible or seemingly magical influence.

core.definition: The practice of magic or supernatural power used to influence events, often considered evil or forbidden by religious traditions.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable. The 'r' is clearly pronounced in American English, and the 'aft' ending rhymes with 'raft'.

nuance.connotation: Negative in most contexts, though some modern users describe it neutrally or positively as a spiritual practice.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use witchcraft in stories, religious talk and everyday descriptions of magic. In casual speech it can also describe something that seems magical, such as 'That's witchcraft!' Be careful, because religious people may find the word sensitive in some conversations.

distinctions.note: Magic is broad and can be entertainment or fantasy; witchcraft is specifically the practice of witches, often with negative religious associations.
Sorcery is more formal and emphasizes spells or dark power; witchcraft is the more common everyday word.

examples.everyday: That old movie had a story about a village where people believed witchcraft caused the bad crops.
examples.professional: Our product team joked that the new algorithm works like witchcraft because nobody understands its results.
examples.analytical: Scripture repeatedly forbids witchcraft, classing it with divination and sorcery as a turning away from the Lord.

nuance.analogy: Witchcraft is like a shadow that claims to hold power over the light; it promises control while hiding its source.
nuance.etymology: From 'witch' (Old English 'wicce', a female sorcerer) plus 'craft' (skill or practice).
common_mistakes: Mispronouncing the 'ch' as a 'k' or a 'sh'; it is a 'ch' as in 'church'.
Using 'witchcraft' as a neutral synonym for all magic in serious religious writing, where it has a specific negative sense.
nuance.biblical_note: Hebrew 'kashaph' (sorcery, the practice of magic) and Greek 'pharmakeia' (sorcery, drug-related magic) describe the forbidden practices. Deuteronomy 18:10-11 forbids Israel from practicing divination, sorcery, or consulting spirits and the dead. Exodus 22:18 says a sorceress should not be allowed to live, showing how seriously the law treated it. Galatians 5:20 lists sorcery among the works of the flesh that are contrary to the Spirit.

witchcraft.etymology: From Middle English *wicchecraft*, *wicchecreft*, from Old English *wiċċecræft*, equivalent to *witch* + *-craft*.

senses.definition: Like, or suiting a wizard.

core.definition: Like a wizard; magical or extraordinarily skillful in a way that seems almost supernatural.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, WIZ. The middle syllable is a weak 'erd' with a reduced r-colored vowel, and the final syllable is 'lee'.

nuance.connotation: Positive. It praises someone's extraordinary skill, often playfully, though it can sound fanciful.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use wizardly playfully in praise, such as 'a wizardly touch with spreadsheets' or 'wizardly cooking'. It is more common in writing and casual compliments than in formal business speech. In a technical team, 'you're a wizard with this code' is a more natural way to say the same thing.

distinctions.note: Magical can describe anything wonderful; wizardly refers specifically to the skill or manner of a wizard.
Masterly praises expertise in a formal way; wizardly is more playful and suggests skill that seems almost supernatural.

examples.everyday: My dad has a wizardly touch with a grill; he can fix anything that goes wrong on a barbecue.
examples.professional: Priya's wizardly handling of the migration saved us a whole weekend of downtime.
examples.analytical: Coleridge's wizardly imagination turns ordinary sensation into vision, a power he describes with suspicion and awe.

nuance.analogy: A wizardly worker is like a skilled magician who makes a hard problem disappear: the trick looks effortless, but it comes from deep training.
nuance.etymology: From wizard (Middle English wysard, a wise man) plus the adjective suffix -ly.
common_mistakes: Using wizardly as a plain adjective for 'technical' work without the playful sense it carries.
Confusing wizardly (adjective) with wizardry (noun) in a sentence.

senses.definition: The quality of being woeful.

core.definition: The state of being sad, miserable, or deplorably poor in quality or condition.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable. Both the -ful and -ness endings are reduced, so say them as 'fuhl' and 'nuhs.' Be careful not to pronounce the o as a long 'oo' sound.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It emphasizes misery or deplorable quality in a weighty, serious way.
nuance.usage_note: Americans rarely use woefulness in speech. It appears mainly in literary writing, formal essays, and occasional commentary on bad situations. In everyday English, sadness, misery, or how bad something is are more natural choices.

distinctions.note: Sadness is a plain, common word for an emotion; woefulness suggests a deeper, more dismal state, often of a whole situation.
Sorrow implies grief, often over a loss; woefulness describes a general condition of misery or poor quality.
Wretchedness is a stronger word for extreme misery or degradation; woefulness is more restrained.

collocations: the sheer woefulness of the results

examples.professional: The quarterly report captured the woefulness of our customer retention numbers without any spin.
examples.analytical: The essay argues that the woefulness of human existence cannot be understood apart from a serious account of sin and its consequences.

nuance.analogy: Woefulness is like a room that stays dim no matter how many lamps you turn on: the gloom seems built into the place itself.
nuance.etymology: From woeful, from woe, plus the noun suffix -ness.
common_mistakes: Writing woefullness with a double l.
Using it in casual speech, where sadness or how bad it was would sound more natural.
Confusing the noun with the adverb woefully when a noun is needed.

senses.definition: (archaic, poetic) Called (by a certain name), named.
senses.label: archaic, poetic

senses.definition: Past participle of clepe.

core.definition: Called by a particular name; named. Used mainly in humorous or mock-archaic writing.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the second syllable and rhyme the ending with 'kept'. The initial 'y' is silent; the word begins with a short 'ih' sound.

nuance.connotation: Neutral
nuance.usage_note: Yclept is archaic and almost never used in spoken American English. You may meet it in older literature, in Shakespeare-style or Spenserian writing, or in humorous phrasing like 'a man yclept Smith'. If you use it, the effect is playful or deliberately old-fashioned; in ordinary speech, say 'called' or 'named'.

distinctions.note: Called is the normal modern word; yclept is archaic and sounds deliberately old-fashioned.
Named is neutral and clear; yclept adds a literary or comic tone.

examples.professional: The report is by a consultant yclept Dr. Lee, though the email signature just says Lee.
examples.analytical: The archaic participle yclept marks a text as deliberately antiquarian, and its use in modern prose signals irony or literary allusion.

nuance.analogy: Like a costume: it gives a sentence an old-fashioned look, but it is not everyday clothing.
nuance.etymology: From Middle English ycleped, from Old English clipian (to call), with the prefix y- from Old English ge-.
common_mistakes: Using yclept in ordinary speech, where 'named' or 'called' is natural
Treating it as a verb form in modern English without the archaic context

yclept.etymology: From Middle English *yclept*, *ycleped*, *iclept* (*i-*, *y-* + *clepen* (“to say, speak, utter; to call, shout; to name; to address; to appeal to, beg, pray; to ask, request; to appear; to send for, summon; to convene; to call forth, induce; to lay…

senses.definition: Really?; no kidding!; is that so?
senses.example: They're going to have a baby? You don't say!

core.definition: An expression of surprise or mild sarcasm at news the listener has just given, meaning 'really?'

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on 'say,' and 'don't' is quick and reduced to 'dohnt.' In speech 'you don't' often blends into 'yoo-DOHNT,' so do not say each word separately.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to sarcastic, depending on tone; a flat delivery can sound mocking.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say 'you don't say' casually, often in a teasing or ironic way when the news is obvious or surprising. A natural reply is 'I know, right?' or 'Right? It was crazy.' Do not use it to a serious speaker who is sharing bad news, as it can sound dismissive.

distinctions.note: Really? is a neutral question asking for confirmation; you don't say is more colorful and often carries a hint of irony.
No way expresses strong disbelief or refusal; you don't say expresses surprise, often with a teasing edge.

examples.everyday: Your sister is moving to Denver? Well, you don't say!
